sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.summary: Introduces the chapter on analysis of walls and retaining structures. Covers the historical context of earth retaining structures (Coulomb 1776, Rankine 1857), their engineering necessity for grade changes and water access, and the chapter's scope: basic earth pressure theories and design principles applicable across the variety of retaining structure types encountered in civil engineering.
sections.body:
Earth retaining structures are among the oldest built structures in the history of civilization. They are necessary to accommodate a change in grade or ground surface elevation over a short distance. Earth retaining structures are also necessary in harbors, shores, and riverbanks to allow easy access to water. Some of the first technical papers in geotechnical engineering concerned theories for calculating earth pressures for retaining structures (Coulomb 1776; Rankine 1857).

Although a myriad of types of earth retaining structures are part of 21st century civil engineering construction, the basic earth pressure theories and major design elements of these structures share common links.

This chapter presents the basic theories and principles behind the calculation of earth pressure. The application of these theories and principles is illustrated for a variety of retaining structures encountered in civil engineering construction.
key_points: Earth retaining structures are among the oldest built structures, required for grade changes and water access.
Foundational earth pressure theories trace to Coulomb (1776) and Rankine (1857).
Despite the variety of retaining structures, basic earth pressure theories and design elements share common links.
This chapter covers calculation of earth pressure and its application to a variety of retaining structures.
sections.applicability: Applies when beginning the study of earth pressure theory and retaining structure design within UFC 3-220-20 Chapter 4.

sections.title: DEVELOPMENT OF EARTH PRESSURES AND LOADS
sections.summary: Parent section covering how earth pressures develop on buried structures (retaining walls, basement walls, ground anchors) as a function of relative movement between the structure and surrounding soil. Introduces the at-rest, active, and passive pressure conditions using the buried-plate analogy, and defines the earth pressure coefficient K as the ratio of horizontal to vertical effective stress.
sections.body:
The earth pressures acting on buried structures, such as retaining walls, basement walls, ground anchors, etc., are dependent on the relative movement between the structure and the surrounding soil. In the simplest form, this is often shown as a buried plate within a soil mass (Figure 4-1). If the plate or structure does not move, then the pressures on the right side and left side of the structure are equal, and this is called an at-rest earth pressure condition. In the at-rest earth pressure condition, the soil is not in a condition of failure.

If a load is applied to the plate to move it toward the right, the soil to the right of the structure is compressed horizontally, and the shear resistance of the soil is mobilized. A passive earth pressure condition develops on the right side. On the left side of the structure, the horizontal stress is decreased, and the soil is extended or stretched until the shear resistance of the soil is mobilized. This is called an active earth pressure condition. The figure also shows how a square element of soil would deform for each of the cases. In the passive zone, the square element is compressed laterally, and in the active zone, the square element is extended laterally. Provided the active and passive conditions are fully developed, the soil is in a condition of failure in both the active and passive zones.

A common parameter used in earth pressure calculations is the earth pressure coefficient, K. The earth pressure coefficient is normally defined as the ratio of the horizontal effective stress to the vertical effective stress at a point within the soil mass. The earth pressure coefficient is occasionally assumed to be the ratio of the horizontal total stress to the vertical total stress. In this chapter, K is defined as the ratio of the effective stresses unless specifically stated otherwise.
key_points: Earth pressures on buried structures depend on relative movement between the structure and the surrounding soil.
At-rest condition (K0): no movement, equal pressures on both sides, soil not at failure.
Active condition: structure moves away from soil; horizontal stress decreases, soil extends to shear failure.
Passive condition: structure moves into soil; horizontal stress increases, soil compresses to shear failure.
Earth pressure coefficient K is defined as the ratio of horizontal to vertical effective stress.
Much more movement is required to develop passive pressures than active pressures.
sections.applicability: Applies to all buried structures (retaining walls, basement walls, ground anchors) where earth pressure calculations are required.

sections.title: At-Rest Earth Pressure
sections.summary: Defines the at-rest earth pressure coefficient K0, its governing equation, and the Mayne and Kulhawy (1982) correlation for estimating K0 from friction angle and overconsolidation ratio (OCR). Covers conditions required for at-rest validity, typical K0 ranges for normally consolidated and overconsolidated soils, and available measurement methods including pressuremeter and dilatometer.
sections.body:
For at-rest conditions, the earth pressure coefficient is defined as:

K0 = σ'h / σ'z  (4-1)

where:
K0 = at-rest earth pressure coefficient,
σ'h = horizontal effective stress, and
σ'z = vertical effective stress.

For this equation to be valid, the soil mass must be in a state of zero lateral strain. Within a soil mass, at-rest conditions normally require a horizontal ground surface and the absence of surface loads of limited areal extent. At-rest conditions can exist when there is a rigid boundary, such as a basement wall, that will satisfy the condition of zero lateral or horizontal strain. For most applications, the horizontal and vertical stresses are the major and minor principal stresses with the relative directions depending on the value of K0 (i.e., σ'h = σ'1 if K0 > 1 and σ'h = σ'3 if K0 < 1).

Standardized laboratory tests are not available to measure the value of K0. Some special test apparatuses have been developed to measure K0 (Filz 1992; Sehn 1990), but these are not used in conventional engineering practice. The Menard pressuremeter, the self-boring pressuremeter, and the Marchetti dilatometer have been used to obtain an in situ measurement of K0, but these devices are not in common use for the design of earth retaining structures.

The most common method used to determine K0 is based on a correlation presented by Mayne and Kulhawy (1982):

K0 = (1 − sin φ') · OCR^(sin φ')  (4-2)

where:
K0 = at-rest earth pressure coefficient,
φ' = effective stress friction angle for normally consolidated conditions, and
OCR = overconsolidation ratio.

K0 values are less than one for normally consolidated soils, and can range from about 0.3 to 0.8. For simple calculations, K0 is often assumed to be equal to 0.5. In overconsolidated soils, it is common for the value of K0 to be greater than one, indicating that the horizontal effective stress is greater than the vertical effective stress.
key_points: K0 is the ratio of horizontal to vertical effective stress under zero lateral strain conditions (Eq. 4-1).
At-rest conditions require horizontal ground surface and absence of localized surface loads.
Standardized laboratory tests for K0 are not available; special apparatus and in-situ devices exist but are uncommon in practice.
Mayne and Kulhawy (1982) correlation (Eq. 4-2) is the most common method: K0 = (1−sin φ')·OCR^(sin φ').
K0 ranges ~0.3–0.8 for normally consolidated soils; often assumed 0.5 for simple calculations.
K0 > 1 is common for overconsolidated soils, indicating horizontal stress exceeds vertical stress.

equations.description: At-rest earth pressure coefficient defined as ratio of horizontal to vertical effective stress: K0 = σ'h / σ'z
Mayne and Kulhawy (1982) correlation for at-rest earth pressure coefficient: K0 = (1 − sin φ') · OCR^(sin φ'), where φ' is the effective friction angle and OCR is the overconsolidation ratio

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating at-rest lateral earth pressure for structures with zero lateral deformation, such as rigid basement walls.

sections.title: Rankine Active and Passive Earth Pressures
sections.summary: Derives Rankine active and passive earth pressure coefficients (KA and KP) from Mohr circle geometry and effective stress friction angle, and presents equations for horizontal effective stress including cohesion. Explains principal stress orientations in active vs. passive states and discusses when the cohesion term is neglected for practical conservatism in both coarse- and fine-grained soils.
sections.body:
Both the active and passive earth pressure coefficients represent the effective stress ratio for a failure condition in the soil. The earth pressure coefficients KA and KP are best explained using Rankine's (1857) earth pressure theory. Mohr circles representing at-rest, active, and passive conditions are shown in Figure 4-2.

For the at-rest conditions, the Mohr circle is not tangent to the envelope; therefore, it does not represent a condition of failure. The circle representing an active failure shows that the horizontal stress is equal to KA multiplied by the vertical stress, and the Mohr circle is tangent to the envelope. The circle representing the passive failure condition shows that the horizontal stress is equal to KP multiplied by the vertical stress. In the active condition, the major principal stress (σ'1) is vertical and the minor principal stress (σ'3) is horizontal. For the passive condition, the major principal stress (σ'1) is horizontal and the minor principal stress (σ'3) is vertical. For both of these cases, the horizontal stress is the earth pressure.

Rankine's theory and the geometry of the Mohr circles shown in Figure 4-2 result in the following equations for the active and passive earth pressure coefficients:

Active: KA = (1 − sin φ') / (1 + sin φ') = tan²(45° − φ'/2)  (4-3)

Passive: KP = (1 + sin φ') / (1 − sin φ') = tan²(45° + φ'/2)  (4-4)

1/KA = KP  (4-5)

where:
KA = coefficient of active earth pressure,
KP = coefficient of passive earth pressure, and
φ' = effective stress friction angle.

The Mohr circles in Figure 4-2 allow the horizontal effective stress to be predicted for both active and passive conditions for the stresses at any point within the failure zone. The horizontal pressures are calculated as:

Active: σ'h = KA · σ'z − 2c' · √KA  (4-6)

Passive: σ'h = KP · σ'z + 2c' · √KP  (4-7)

where:
KA = coefficient of active earth pressure,
KP = coefficient of passive earth pressure,
σ'h = horizontal effective stress (earth pressure),
σ'z = vertical effective stress, and
c' = effective stress cohesion intercept.

From Equations 4-6 and 4-7, the effective cohesion intercept theoretically decreases the active earth pressure and increases the passive earth pressure. The value of c' is usually assumed to be zero for coarse-grained soils. Fine-grained soils that are represented by a linear failure envelope may have a value of c', which is associated with overconsolidation or compaction. These soils creep, shrink, and swell with time, and the operating value of c' can decrease or reach zero. For this reason, the changes to the earth pressures caused by c' are usually neglected for fine-grained soils.
key_points: KA and KP represent effective stress ratios at failure; Mohr circles for active/passive states are tangent to the strength envelope.
Active: KA = (1−sin φ')/(1+sin φ') = tan²(45°−φ'/2); σ'1 is vertical (Eq. 4-3).
Passive: KP = (1+sin φ')/(1−sin φ') = tan²(45°+φ'/2); σ'1 is horizontal (Eq. 4-4).
KA and KP are reciprocals: 1/KA = KP (Eq. 4-5).
Cohesion c' reduces active pressure and increases passive pressure per Eqs. 4-6 and 4-7.
c' is typically assumed zero for coarse-grained soils; neglected for fine-grained soils due to creep and volume change effects.

equations.description: Rankine active earth pressure coefficient: KA = (1 − sin φ') / (1 + sin φ') = tan²(45° − φ'/2)
Rankine passive earth pressure coefficient: KP = (1 + sin φ') / (1 − sin φ') = tan²(45° + φ'/2)
Reciprocal relationship between active and passive coefficients: 1/KA = KP
Rankine horizontal effective stress for active condition including cohesion: σ'h = KA · σ'z − 2c' · √KA
Rankine horizontal effective stress for passive condition including cohesion: σ'h = KP · σ'z + 2c' · √KP

sections.applicability: Applies when calculating active or passive horizontal effective stress using Rankine theory for soils with a linear Mohr-Coulomb failure envelope.

sections.title: Movement Required to Develop Active and Passive States
sections.summary: Discusses the wall displacement (translation or rotation) required to fully mobilize active and passive earth pressure conditions. Passive pressures require 5–10× more displacement than active. Covers variation by soil type (dense vs. loose sand, compacted clay) and notes that theoretical KA and KP values in clay can only be sustained short-term due to creep.
sections.body:
An important consideration in earth pressure theory is the amount of movement required to develop the active and passive earth pressure conditions. Much more movement or displacement is required to develop the passive condition than the active condition. This is particularly important in the design of earth retention structures or soil anchors since both active and passive pressures affect the performance of the structure. However, the amount of displacement of the structure might not be an explicit parameter in the calculations.

Figure 4-3(a) illustrates the importance of wall movement on the development of active and passive earth pressures. For active and passive pressures to fully develop, the wall must translate laterally or tilt (rotate). The figure shows general trends developed from experimental data linking the magnitude of the earth pressure coefficient to wall rotation, expressed as the ratio of horizontal displacement (Y) to the wall height (H). Typical magnitudes for different soil types are summarized in Figure 4-3(d). About five to ten times more displacement is required to develop passive pressures than active pressures.

The amount of displacement required to mobilize active and passive states also depends on the soil type and compaction. Dense sands require less displacement than loose sands. Compacted clays require five to ten times more movement than dense sands. As noted in Figure 4-3(d), theoretical values of KA and KP can only be sustained for short time periods by clay soils because of creep.
key_points: Passive earth pressure requires approximately 5–10× more wall displacement to mobilize than active earth pressure.
Wall movement can be translational or rotational; wall rotation Y/H is the normalized displacement parameter.
Dense sands require less displacement to mobilize active/passive states than loose sands.
Compacted clays require 5–10× more movement than dense sands to develop active/passive pressures.
Theoretical KA and KP values can only be sustained short-term in clay due to creep.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating whether sufficient wall movement exists to mobilize active or passive earth pressure conditions in retaining structure design.

sections.title: Earth Pressure Distributions and Loads
sections.summary: Describes triangular active and passive earth pressure distributions on retaining walls using Rankine theory for horizontal backfill with no wall friction or cohesion, and presents the resultant force equations (PA and PP) as functions of K, unit weight, and wall height. Notes equations apply to drained (effective stress) conditions and flags important issues with undrained application discussed in Section 4-3.3.
sections.body:
Figure 4-3(b) and (c) illustrate the active and passive pressure distributions acting on a retaining wall. The earth pressure is calculated over the depth of the backfill (H). The cases shown have horizontal backfill, no effective stress cohesion, and no friction between the wall and backfill. The active and passive earth pressures result in triangular pressure distributions.

The resultant force of the triangular pressure distribution is determined for the active and passive cases as:

Active: PA = KA · γ · H² / 2  (4-8)

Passive: PP = KP · γ · H² / 2  (4-9)

where:
PA = active earth pressure resultant force,
PP = passive earth pressure resultant force,
γ = unit weight of backfill soil, and
H = height of wall.

The equations shown above are for effective stress or drained analyses. The same equations can be expressed for undrained or total stress analyses. For this case, total stress strength parameters (c, φ, or su) are used in the equations, and the calculated earth pressure is the total horizontal stress (σh). There are some important issues regarding the application of the Rankine method to undrained or total stress conditions, which are discussed in Section 4-3.3.

Figure 4-4 shows earth pressure distributions for active and passive cases using the Rankine theory. The application of the Rankine theory is generally limited to cases where there is not any friction between the retaining wall and the soil (i.e., smooth wall) and the backfill is horizontal although there are published techniques that can accommodate inclined backfills.
key_points: Rankine earth pressure distributions are triangular for horizontal backfill with no wall friction and no cohesion.
Active resultant: PA = KA·γ·H²/2 (Eq. 4-8); Passive resultant: PP = KP·γ·H²/2 (Eq. 4-9).
These equations apply to drained (effective stress) analyses; total stress versions use c, φ, or su.
Rankine theory is limited to smooth walls (no wall friction) and horizontal backfill, though inclined backfill techniques exist.
Application to undrained/total stress conditions has important caveats covered in Section 4-3.3.

equations.description: Active earth pressure resultant force for triangular pressure distribution: PA = KA · γ · H² / 2
Passive earth pressure resultant force for triangular pressure distribution: PP = KP · γ · H² / 2

sections.applicability: Applies when computing resultant active and passive earth pressure forces on retaining walls with horizontal backfill, no wall friction, and no cohesion under drained conditions.

sections.title: Rankine Method Examples
sections.summary: Presents worked examples of active and passive Rankine earth pressure calculations for a wall with horizontal backfill, uniform surcharge, no wall friction, and uneven water table elevations. Demonstrates use of moist unit weights above and buoyant unit weights below the water table, and application of the cohesion term. Figures 4-5 and 4-6 show the full calculation diagrams for active and passive cases respectively.
sections.body:
Figure 4-5 shows an example for active pressure determination using the Rankine method for the following conditions:
• horizontal backfill,
• uniform surcharge load (q),
• no wall friction,
• horizontal water surfaces on both sides of the wall, and
• homogeneous soil conditions with strength characterized by c' and φ'.

For this example, moist unit weights are used above the water table and buoyant unit weights are used below the water table in order to calculate the correct vertical effective stress. In this example, the earth pressure caused by the surcharge is greater than the reduction in earth pressure due to the effects of cohesion, so the earth pressure at the ground surface is greater than zero. It is common to ignore the contribution of the cohesion term in earth pressure calculations for additional conservatism.

Figure 4-6 has the same cross section as Figure 4-5, but the equations for passive earth pressure are shown. The calculations are very similar to the active earth pressure example (Figure 4-5).
key_points: Moist unit weights apply above the water table; buoyant unit weights apply below the water table for vertical effective stress calculation.
Uniform surcharge load q adds a uniform earth pressure increment = KA·q for active case.
Cohesion term reduces active earth pressure; it is commonly neglected for conservatism.
Passive example (Figure 4-6) mirrors active example (Figure 4-5) with KP substituted for KA.
Water table level on each side of the wall must be tracked separately for correct effective stress.
sections.applicability: Applies when performing step-by-step Rankine earth pressure calculations for walls with surcharge loads, cohesive soils, and uneven water table elevations on each side.

sections.title: Wall/Soil Interface Friction Angle
sections.summary: Covers the wall/soil interface friction angle δ, how it is measured in direct shear tests with wall material in the bottom shear box half, and how to obtain typical δ values from Table 4-1 for concrete, masonry, and steel sheet pile walls against various soil types. Also introduces adhesion Ca for clayey soils at wall interfaces as an alternative undrained resistance parameter.
sections.body: The interface friction angle (δ) between the wall and soil backfill can be an important parameter in retaining wall analysis. The angle is equal to that obtained in a direct shear apparatus when the bottom half of the shear box is the wall material (normally concrete or steel) and the top half is soil. Tests can be conducted at pressures in the same range as the earth pressures, and a linear envelope is fit through the data. In geotechnical practice, these special direct shear tests are not often conducted, and the value of δ is most often obtained from published data, such as that presented in Table 4-1. Typical δ values for various combinations of wall materials and soil types are provided. For clayey soils located at an interface, such as the bottom of a wall or adjacent to a sheet pile, the resistance is termed the adhesion, Ca.
key_points: Interface friction angle δ is measured in a direct shear test with wall material in the bottom shear box half and soil in the top half.
Special direct shear tests for δ are uncommon in practice; values are typically obtained from published tables (Table 4-1).
Table 4-1 provides δ values and friction factors (tan δ) for mass concrete/masonry, steel sheet piles, and formed concrete against a range of soil types.
For clayey soils at interfaces, the resistance parameter is adhesion Ca (in psf), not a friction angle.
Adhesion Ca values in Table 4-1 range from 0 to 1300 psf depending on undrained shear strength of the fine-grained soil.
Interface friction angle δ is important when wall roughness must be considered (e.g., Coulomb method), as Rankine assumes smooth walls.
sections.applicability: Applies when the wall/soil interface friction angle δ or adhesion Ca is needed for retaining wall design, particularly for Coulomb-based earth pressure methods or base sliding calculations.

sections.title: Active and Passive Earth Pressure from Other Methods
sections.summary: Introduces alternative earth pressure calculation methods beyond Rankine — specifically the Coulomb trial wedge method and the log spiral method. Explains that these methods accommodate sloping backfills, wall friction, irregular surcharges, and sloping wall faces that cannot be handled by Rankine's KA and KP equations (Eq. 4-3 and 4-4).
sections.body: The values of KA and KP for the Rankine method, as presented in Equations 4-3 and 4-4, are solely a function of the drained friction angle, φʹ. Other methods of calculating earth pressure coefficients, such as the trial wedge method developed by Coulomb (1776) and the log spiral method summarized by Caquot and Kerisel (1948), are available. With the trial wedge and log spiral methods, the effects of other factors, such as sloping backfills and wall friction, can be accommodated, and these effects are reflected in the values of the earth pressure coefficients. A gravity retaining wall with a sloping backfill (β) and wall (θ) is shown in Figure 4-7 for a case where the wall/soil interface friction angle (δ) is considered.
key_points: Rankine KA and KP depend only on φʹ; other methods extend this to include wall friction, backfill slope, and irregular geometry.
Coulomb (1776) trial wedge method and Caquot & Kerisel (1948) log spiral method are the principal alternatives.
Wall/soil interface friction angle (δ), backfill slope (β), and wall face slope (θ) are key additional parameters.
Figure 4-7 illustrates the geometry of a gravity retaining wall with sloping backfill, sloping wall, and interface friction.
sections.applicability: Applies when Rankine method is insufficient due to sloping backfills, wall friction, irregular surcharges, or sloping wall faces.

sections.title: Coulomb Wedge Method
sections.summary: Describes Coulomb's (1776) limit equilibrium trial wedge method for computing active and passive earth pressure forces. Covers its advantages over Rankine (irregular surfaces, wall friction, surcharges), the graphical/chart/equation solution approaches, and provides closed-form equations for active (Eq. 4-10) and passive (Eq. 4-11) earth pressure forces for sloping walls with interface friction. Also addresses the negative δ case for settling walls.
sections.body:
Coulomb (1776) developed a limit equilibrium method for calculating the force applied to a wall or anchor for the active and passive earth pressure conditions. This method, along with other modifications of the method, analyzes the forces acting on an active or passive failure wedge defined by a linear failure surface. The main differences between the active and passive cases are the angle at which the resultant force acts on the wall and the direction of the shear forces acting on the failure plane, owing to the difference in the direction of movement of the wedge.

The Coulomb method has advantages over the Rankine method in that it can accommodate:
• irregular ground surfaces,
• sloping wall faces,
• irregular surcharge loads on the ground surface, and
• interface friction between the wall and the soil backfill.

A Coulomb analysis can be performed as a graphical solution, chart solution, or equations can be developed for direct calculations. Different failure surfaces are analyzed until the maximum active force or minimum passive force is obtained. The free body diagrams and force polygons for the active and passive conditions for cases with and without wall friction are shown in Figure 4-8.

For the conditions given in Figure 4-8(a), Figure 4-9 provides values of KA and KP for different friction angles and backfill slopes, assuming cʹ = 0. Once the earth pressure coefficient has been determined, then a resultant force (PA or PP) can be calculated using the same procedure as used for the Rankine method (Equations 4-8 and 4-9). Figure 4-10 allows the determination of the slope of the linear failure surface measured from vertical (α).

The active earth pressure load can be directly calculated for the more complex case of a sloping wall face (θ), sloping backfill (β), and interface friction angle (δ) as:

PA = (1/2) · γ · H² · cos²(φʹ − θ) / { cos²θ · cos(θ + δ) · [1 + sqrt( sin(φʹ + δ)sin(φʹ − β) / (cos(θ + δ)cos(θ − β)) )]² }

where:
PA = active earth pressure force,
γ = unit weight of backfill soil,
H = wall height,
φʹ = effective stress or drained friction angle,
θ = slope angle of the wall face,
δ = interface friction angle between wall and soil, and
β = slope of backfill surface.

The passive earth pressure load can be calculated as:

PP = (1/2) · γ · H² · cos²(φʹ + θ) / { cos²θ · cos(θ − δ) · [1 − sqrt( sin(φʹ + δ)sin(φʹ + β) / (cos(θ − δ)cos(θ − β)) )]² }

where:
KP = passive earth pressure force.

For cases with surcharge loads, irregular backfill slopes, line loads, etc., the individual forces in the free body diagram (FBD) should be calculated, and force equilibrium should be used to find the values of PA and PP for trial failure surfaces. In addition, for active earth pressure cases where the wall is expected to settle a significant amount, it may be necessary to reverse the direction of the shear force on the wall in the FBD. This is called a negative δ case, and the reversal of the direction of the shear force is detrimental to wall stability.
key_points: Coulomb method uses a linear failure surface and limit equilibrium to find maximum active or minimum passive force.
Advantages over Rankine: handles irregular ground, sloping walls, surcharges, and wall/soil interface friction.
Eq. 4-10 gives active force PA for sloping wall, sloping backfill, and interface friction; Eq. 4-11 gives passive force PP.
Figures 4-9 and 4-10 provide chart solutions for KA, KP, and failure plane angle for vertical walls without wall friction.
For complex cases (surcharges, irregular layers), individual FBD forces must be resolved for each trial surface.
Negative δ case applies when the wall settles significantly, reversing wall shear direction, which is detrimental to stability.

equations.description: Coulomb active earth pressure force PA for sloping wall face (θ), sloping backfill (β), and interface friction angle (δ): PA = (1/2)·γ·H²·cos²(φʹ−θ) / { cos²θ·cos(θ+δ)·[1+sqrt(sin(φʹ+δ)sin(φʹ−β)/(cos(θ+δ)cos(θ−β)))]² }

Coulomb passive earth pressure force PP for sloping wall face (θ), sloping backfill (β), and interface friction angle (δ): PP = (1/2)·γ·H²·cos²(φʹ+θ) / { cos²θ·cos(θ−δ)·[1−sqrt(sin(φʹ+δ)sin(φʹ+β)/(cos(θ−δ)cos(θ−β)))]² }

sections.applicability: Applies when calculating active or passive earth pressure forces on retaining walls with sloping faces, sloping backfills, wall friction, or irregular surcharge conditions.

sections.title: Log Spiral Method
sections.summary: Explains that the true failure surface is curved (log spiral), not linear, making Coulomb unconservative for passive resistance especially when δ/φʹ > 0.4. Presents Eq. 4-12 for approximating log spiral Kp for vertical walls with horizontal backfill, references charts (Figures 4-12, 4-13) based on Kerisel and Absi (1990), and Table 4-2 comparing Rankine, Coulomb, and log spiral KA/KP values across friction angles.
sections.body:
One simplification of the Rankine and Coulomb methods is the assumption of a linear failure plane. Experimental and numerical analysis have shown that the true failure surface is curved instead of linear. The surface closely approximates a logarithmic spiral. The linear and log spiral failure surfaces for the active and passive earth pressure cases are shown in Figure 4-11. The difference in the failure planes is not substantial for the active earth pressure case, but there is a considerable difference in the passive case. If the Coulomb method is used to calculate the passive resistance of an earth anchor, the resistance will be greatly overestimated compared to results using the log spiral method. Much less soil is engaged by the true, log spiral surface compared to the linear Coulomb surface. This is especially true as the interface friction angle approaches the friction angle of the soil (i.e., δ/φʹ > 0.4). Therefore, passive pressure should be calculated using the log spiral method and not the Coulomb method.

Unfortunately, the calculations for the log spiral method are not as simple as for the Coulomb method. Caquot and Kerisel (1948) provide tables of values of KA and KP for different wall geometries and interface friction angles. Alqarawi et al. (2021) provide the equations for using a spreadsheet to perform log spiral analysis calculations. Alternatively, charts can be used to determine values of KA and KP for log spiral solutions.

Figure 4-12 shows values of KA and KP for the log spiral method for walls with a sloping face and δ/φʹ = 0.66 based on the published data of Kerisel and Absi (1990). Figure 4-13 is a similar chart for vertical-faced walls having a sloping backfill.

The log spiral method is commonly used for cut walls, such as sheet pile or soldier pile and lagging, where both KA and KP are required. These walls are vertical and often have no backslope. While δ/φʹ = 0.66 is a common assumption, this type of design may require Kp for a different value of wall friction. For conditions with θ = 0 deg and β = 0 deg, the value of Kp can be approximated as:

Kp = (1 + sin φʹ) / (1 − sin φʹ) · exp( (δ/φʹ) · ln( (1 + sin φʹ) / (1 − sin φʹ) ) · 1.443 · sin φʹ )

where:
Kp = log spiral passive earth pressure coefficient for θ = 0 deg and β = 0 deg,
φʹ = effective stress friction angle, and
δ = wall-soil interface friction angle.

As expected, Equation 4-12 results in the Rankine value of Kp if wall friction is neglected.

Table 4-2 compares KA and KP values calculated by the Rankine, Coulomb, and Log Spiral methods for a range of friction angles and δ/φʹ values. Examining the active case, the method and wall friction have little effect on the predicted KA. In most cases, the Rankine method is appropriate for active conditions without sloping wall or backfill. For the passive case, the earth pressure theory and wall friction have a large impact on the magnitude of the predicted KP. The log spiral KP can be in the range of two to five times higher than the Rankine value. This is especially important for the design of cut-type retaining walls, such as sheet pile and soldier pile, that rely on passive earth pressures for stability.
key_points: True failure surface is curved (log spiral), not linear; Coulomb significantly overestimates passive resistance when δ/φʹ > 0.4.
Log spiral method should always be used for passive pressure calculations, especially for earth anchors and cut walls.
Eq. 4-12 approximates log spiral Kp for vertical walls with horizontal backfill (θ = 0°, β = 0°) as a function of φʹ and δ.
Figures 4-12 and 4-13 provide log spiral KA and KP charts based on Kerisel and Absi (1990) for δ/φʹ = 0.66.
Table 4-2 shows log spiral Kp can be 2–5× greater than Rankine Kp; Coulomb Kp values in parentheses are unconservative and should not be used.
KA is relatively insensitive to method and wall friction; Rankine is generally adequate for active conditions on simple geometry.
Note: Figures 4-12 and 4-13 differ significantly from DM 7.2 (1982) charts, which used δ/φʹ = 1 with reduction ratios.

equations.description: Log spiral passive earth pressure coefficient Kp for θ = 0° and β = 0°: Kp = exp[ (δ/φʹ) · ln((1+sinφʹ)/(1−sinφʹ)) · 1.443·sinφʹ ] · (1+sinφʹ)/(1−sinφʹ), where φʹ = effective friction angle and δ = wall-soil interface friction angle.

sections.applicability: Applies when calculating passive earth pressure for cut walls (sheet pile, soldier pile), earth anchors, or any case where δ/φʹ > 0.4, where Coulomb method is unconservatively large.

sections.title: Presumptive Earth Pressure Coefficients and Equivalent Fluid Pressures
sections.summary: Addresses practical limitations of theory-based earth pressures: fine-grained soil creep can increase active loads and decrease passive loads over time. Presents presumptive earth pressure coefficients and equivalent fluid unit weights (Table 4-3) for at-rest and yielding conditions for various soil types. Defines Eq. 4-13 for γeq and Eq. 4-14 for horizontal pressure including surcharge. Limits use to walls ≤ 20 feet tall.
sections.body:
The earth pressure theories presented within this section are based on the shear strength of the backfill material. Pressures imparted by water and other loads applied to the backfill will be discussed in Section 4-4. A few additional factors that may impact the loads applied to retaining structures are discussed below.

In particular, fine-grained soils can creep. There are many definitions for creep in the geotechnical literature, but the term usually refers to a time-dependent deformation of a soil at a constant effective stress. For structures constructed to retain fine-grained soils, the active earth loads applied to the structure can increase over time to values that significantly exceed the loads calculated by earth pressure theory. Similarly, passive earth loads may decrease over time in fine-grained soils. For this reason, presumptive earth pressure coefficients that empirically incorporate the effects of creep are often an appropriate alternative to values based on earth pressure theory.

In addition, the typical design and construction sequence imposes another practical constraint on the calculation of earth pressures and loads. Gravity retaining walls are often designed prior to the selection of a specific backfill material with well-defined properties (e.g., φʹ and γ). In this case, presumptive earth pressure coefficients will be just as accurate as design based on assumed values of φʹ and γ.

Presumptive values based on relative density and soil type are provided in Table 4-3 for both at-rest and yielding wall conditions. These values can be used to account for the effects of creep as well as the constraints of the design and construction process.

For the case of no backfill surcharge, the earth pressure applied to retaining structures has a triangular pressure distribution. For this reason, it is often convenient to use the equivalent fluid unit weight, γeq, to calculate earth pressures using the same methodology as for hydrostatic fluids. The equivalent fluid unit weight is found as:

γeq = K · γ

where:
γ = the unit weight of the backfill and
K = an appropriate earth pressure coefficient (at-rest or active).

Table 4-3 shows values of γeq for horizontal and sloped backfills for different backfill soil types. The effects of creep are reflected in the γeq values for the clay backfill materials. The choice of the value of the equivalent fluid unit weight should consider wall movement and the potential of the backfill soil to creep over time. Since equivalent fluid pressures are only an approximate method to calculate earth pressures, their use should be limited to walls that are less than 20 feet tall.

A uniform surface surcharge (discussed in more detail in Section 4-4.2) can also be considered using presumptive earth pressures. Using the appropriate values listed in Table 4-3, the horizontal earth pressure at the bottom of the wall, σh, can be calculated as:

σh = γeq · z + K · q

where:
γeq = equivalent fluid unit weight,
z = depth below ground surface,
K = horizontal earth pressure coefficient, and
q = uniform surcharge pressure.
key_points: Creep in fine-grained soils can cause active earth loads to exceed theory-based values over time; passive loads may decrease.
Presumptive earth pressure coefficients (Table 4-3) empirically incorporate creep and are useful when backfill properties are unknown at design time.
Equivalent fluid unit weight γeq = K·γ (Eq. 4-13) simplifies earth pressure to a hydrostatic analogy for triangular distributions.
Eq. 4-14 adds uniform surcharge contribution: σh = γeq·z + K·q.
Table 4-3 provides γeq and K values for at-rest and active conditions for loose/medium/dense sand/gravel, compacted silt, lean clay, and fat clay, for both level and 2H:1V sloping backfills.
Use of equivalent fluid pressures is limited to walls less than 20 feet tall.

equations.description: Equivalent fluid unit weight: γeq = K · γ, where γ = unit weight of backfill and K = earth pressure coefficient (at-rest or active).

Horizontal earth pressure at depth z with uniform surcharge: σh = γeq · z + K · q, where γeq = equivalent fluid unit weight, z = depth below ground surface, K = horizontal earth pressure coefficient, and q = uniform surcharge pressure.

sections.applicability: Applies to retaining walls less than 20 feet tall retaining fine-grained or granular soils where creep effects are a concern or backfill properties are not yet defined at design time.

sections.title: Earth Pressure Examples for Complex Geometries
sections.summary: Presents worked examples of the Coulomb trial wedge method applied to complex cross-sections with uneven backfill surfaces, irregular surcharges, multiple soil layers, non-horizontal water tables, and wall friction. Figure 4-14 covers active pressure; Figure 4-15 covers passive pressure using a circular arc to approximate the log spiral. Discusses use of limit equilibrium and FEM/FDM software for such problems.
sections.body:
A more complex active pressure problem is shown in Figure 4-14. In this case, the surface of the backfill is uneven, and an irregular surcharge is present. Two different soil types are present, and the contact between these soils is not horizontal. The ground water table is not horizontal, which means it is a hydrodynamic case (e.g., water is flowing). Friction between the wall and backfill will be considered.

The type of problem shown in Figure 4-14 is too complicated for the Rankine method, and the Coulomb method must be used. In addition, the problem is too complex for the Coulomb charts (Figure 4-9 and Figure 4-10), and different trial failure surfaces must be analyzed by hand. The figure shows the FBDs and force polygons for two trial surfaces.

In this example, the moist unit weight should be used above the water table and the saturated unit weight should be used below the water table when calculating the weight of the wedge. The water pressure force, acting normal to the failure surface, must be calculated. Since two soil types are present, the active wedge is subdivided into two free bodies, with the vertical boundary between the free bodies defined by the location where the layer interface crosses the failure plane. The forces acting on the vertical boundary are assumed to be horizontal.

Figure 4-15 shows a passive pressure example with a cross-section very similar to Figure 4-14. Since wall friction is considered in this example, it would be unconservative to use the linear failure surface assumed by the Coulomb method. Ideally, the log spiral method would be used to solve this problem. However, in this example, a simpler procedure is adopted where the portion of the failure surface that would normally be represented by a log spiral has been replaced with a circular arc. Three free bodies are used in the example solution separated by two vertical boundaries. One boundary between the free bodies has been defined where the circular failure surface transitions into the linear failure surface. The second boundary is located where the interface between the two layers intersects the linear failure surface. The passive earth force for this example is determined by resolving the forces for the three force polygons. To determine the vertical location of the passive force on the wall, moments should be summed about the toe of the wall.

For earth pressure problems that exhibit complex cross-sections, such as those in Figure 4-14 and Figure 4-15, other methods can be used to determine the passive earth pressure. Some limit equilibrium slope stability software can be employed to solve earth pressure problems, and these programs can easily accommodate different soil layering and nonhorizontal contact surfaces. However, the results from these programs should be carefully checked against hand calculations for simpler cross-sections to verify that the user is correctly using the computer software. Also, finite element and finite difference soil structure interaction software can be used to solve these types of problems, but considerable skill is required to obtain meaningful results.
key_points: Complex active pressure problems (irregular backfill, multiple soil layers, non-horizontal water table, wall friction) require hand trial wedge analysis using FBDs and force polygons.
Use moist unit weight above the water table and saturated unit weight below; include water pressure force normal to the failure surface.
For layered soils, subdivide the wedge into multiple free bodies with vertical boundaries; inter-body forces assumed horizontal.
For passive pressure with wall friction, circular arc can replace the log spiral portion of the failure surface as a practical simplification.
Passive force location: sum moments about the wall toe to find the vertical point of application.
Limit equilibrium slope stability software can handle complex earth pressure problems but must be validated against hand calculations.
FEM/FDM soil-structure interaction software can also be used but requires considerable skill for meaningful results.
sections.applicability: Applies to retaining wall earth pressure calculations involving complex geometry: irregular backfill, multiple soil layers, non-horizontal groundwater, irregular surcharges, and wall friction, where standard charts and simple equations are insufficient.

sections.title: Use of Slope Stability Software for Earth Pressures
sections.summary: Explains how limit equilibrium-based slope stability software can be applied to determine earth forces on retaining structures under complex site conditions. Covers five scenarios where software is especially useful (nonlinear strength envelopes, hydrodynamic conditions, layered stratigraphy, nonlinear failure surfaces, tension cracks) and describes the methodology for applying the approach.
sections.body:
Many of the procedures outlined thus far in this manual use the limit equilibrium procedure to determine the forces acting on retaining structures. This is the same basic analysis technique used by most slope stability software. In the hands of an engineer skilled in its use, slope stability software can be used to find the earth forces acting on a retaining structure for complex site conditions. This approach can accommodate more scenarios than the equations and chart solutions normally used in engineering practice.

Situations where slope stability software can be particularly useful are:
1) The shear strength of the backfill soil is more accurately represented by a nonlinear strength envelope as opposed to a linear failure envelope,
2) Hydrodynamic groundwater conditions (as opposed to hydrostatic conditions),
3) Layered soil stratigraphy,
4) Nonlinear failure surfaces in the backfill, and
5) Presence of tension cracks.

Slope stability software can be used for retaining wall analysis by applying the earth pressure force as a line load on the structure at the approximate vertical location. The trial slip surface can be forced to intersect a point at the heel of the wall. Next, the earth pressure force is varied until a factor of safety of unity is achieved. The slope stability method should solve all conditions of equilibrium, such as Spencer's method or the Morgenstern and Price method.

Although the software manual may include examples of retaining wall analysis, the user should be confident in their abilities to do this sort of analysis prior to attempting a design. The results of simple example problems using log-spiral solutions should be compared to computer solutions before more complicated strength models and geometries are analyzed.
key_points: Slope stability software uses the same limit equilibrium basis as hand-calculation earth pressure methods, making it applicable to retaining wall analysis.
Five key scenarios favor software over closed-form solutions: nonlinear strength envelopes, hydrodynamic groundwater, layered stratigraphy, nonlinear failure surfaces, and tension cracks.
Analysis procedure: apply earth pressure as a line load, force slip surface through wall heel, vary earth pressure force until FS = 1.0.
Use methods that satisfy all equilibrium conditions (e.g., Spencer's method, Morgenstern and Price method).
Validate computer solutions against log-spiral hand solutions for simple cases before analyzing complex geometries.
sections.applicability: Applies when using slope stability software to determine earth pressures on retaining structures under complex site conditions not well-handled by standard equations or charts.

sections.title: Earth Pressures from Other Sources
sections.summary: Container section covering earth pressure contributions beyond conventional soil wedge or Rankine/Coulomb approaches, specifically addressing water pressure effects on retaining structures including static water, extreme rainfall events, and seepage beneath cantilever walls.
key_points: Covers earth pressure contributions from sources other than standard dry or moist backfill, primarily water-related loads.
Subsections address static water pressure, extreme rainfall with drainage layers, and seepage beneath cantilever sheet pile walls.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or analyzing retaining structures subject to water pressure, rainfall events, or seepage conditions.

sections.title: Water Pressure Effects
sections.summary: Covers the substantial forces water can exert on retaining structures, including static ponded water (triangular pressure at 62.4 pcf, K=1), the dual effect of elevated water tables (reduced effective stress plus added water pressure), rainfall event pore pressures with drainage layers, and seepage corrections for cantilever sheet pile walls in coarse-grained soils. References Figure 4-16(a), (b), and (c).
sections.body:
Water ponded on the interior of a retaining structure can apply substantial forces to the structure. Water applies a triangular pressure distribution equivalent to a soil with a unit weight of 62.4 pcf and an earth pressure coefficient of unity. The examples given in Figure 4-5 and Figure 4-6 show the net water pressure distribution when there are unequal water elevations on the front and back of the structure.

Because of the large pressures that water can apply to walls, significant efforts are required to prevent water from collecting behind retaining structures. Wall drainage systems are presented in Section 4-5.2. Although water behind a wall creates additional loading, there are many design cases where water loads on walls are unavoidable. Many walls used in waterfront structures have an elevated water level on the ground side compared to the water side. This is also often the case for lock structures on navigable rivers. Sometimes, the drainage system behind a wall can be overwhelmed by significant rainfall events, and the wall may experience potentially damaging, albeit temporary, water loads. Clogging of drainage systems can also lead to damaging water loads.

When the soil behind a wall becomes saturated, the pressure on the wall is controlled by two factors. First, the earth pressure is reduced since the effective stress is decreased. Instead of the total unit weight (γ), the buoyant or effective unit weight (γb) is used in the earth pressure equations for soils below the water table. The second effect is that an additional load, supplied by the water pressure, is applied to the wall. Figure 4-16(a) shows combined influence of these two effects. The consequence of an increasing water level is expressed as a ratio of the height of water (Hw) to the height of the wall (H). When Hw = H, the water level is at the ground surface. The relative increase in the pressure applied to the wall is quantified in the upper right inset as the ratio of the sum of the earth pressure and water pressure force divided by the earth pressure force for Hw = H. As the friction angle increases, this ratio increases.

Figure 4-16(b) shows an analysis case demonstrating the effects of a large rainfall event on the stability of a retaining wall that contains a drainage layer next to the wall. Even with the drainage system installed, a large rainfall event can still increase the pore pressure in the backfill. The flow net shows the head loss as a function of depth. For a potential failure plane, oriented at the angle αA (measured from vertical), the pore pressure distribution can be calculated, and the resulting pore pressure force, U, can be determined. The middle inset shows the ratio of the pore pressure force to the force that would be applied for hydrostatic conditions for different failure plane angles. As the angle of the failure plane increases, the relative water pressure force also increases. The right inset shows the increase in the force applied to the wall, expressed as a ratio of the force calculated from both soil and water for the rainfall event to the active earth pressure force for the case of no water pressures. As the friction angle of the soil increases, this ratio also increases.

For waterfront and riverfront earth retaining structures, active seepage can be occurring, and this can compromise stability. Figure 4-16(c) shows a cantilever sheet pile wall installed in a coarse-grained soil. The water levels are higher on the landside of the wall than on the riverside; therefore, water flow is occurring from right to left. As shown on the figure, the active and passive earth and water pressures should first be calculated assuming conditions of "no flow." Next, corrections to the active and passive pressures can be made to account for the seepage conditions. The correction factors depend on the ratio of the length of the sheeting (H+D) to the depth of embedment and the earth pressure coefficient. The development of the passive pressure occurs at a much greater wall displacement than the active pressure. For cantilever walls, which must include passive pressure, this can be accommodated by a reduction in the value of KP used in the analysis. Cantilever sheet pile design is covered in more detail in Section 4-7.4.
key_points: Water applies a triangular pressure distribution equivalent to γ = 62.4 pcf with K = 1.0; unequal water elevations on each side of a wall produce a net pressure.
Saturated backfill creates two competing effects: reduced earth pressure (buoyant unit weight γb replaces total unit weight γ) plus an added water pressure load.
The combined earth + water pressure force can significantly exceed the dry active earth pressure force, especially at higher soil friction angles.
Even with a drainage layer, extreme rainfall events increase pore pressures along the failure plane; pore pressure force U relative to hydrostatic increases with failure plane angle αA.

For waterfront/riverfront walls with active seepage, 'no flow' active and passive pressures are computed first, then corrected for seepage using factors depending on sheeting length ratio (H+D)/D and earth pressure coefficient.
Passive pressure mobilizes at much larger wall displacements than active pressure; for cantilever sheet pile walls this is handled by reducing KP in the analysis.
Drainage system clogging or overwhelm by rainfall can impose temporary but potentially damaging water loads on retaining walls.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or evaluating retaining structures subject to ponded water, saturated backfill, extreme rainfall events with drainage layers, or active seepage at waterfront/riverfront sites.

sections.title: Surface Loads Behind Retaining Structures
sections.summary: Covers the types of surface loads applied to backfill behind retaining structures and their pressure effects on the wall. Addresses surcharge, rectangular, point, and line loads. Notes that elastic-theory-based solutions assume a rigid, unyielding wall, and that 75% of calculated load may be used when active conditions develop. Discusses practical design considerations for urban construction.
sections.body:
Loads applied to the ground surface behind a retaining structure can impose a pressure distribution to the wall. The types of loads considered here are:
1) Surcharge loading (wide extent compared to wall),
2) Rectangular or surcharge loading over limited area,
3) Point loads,
4) Line loads parallel to wall, and
5) Line loads perpendicular to the wall.

Many of these solutions are based on elastic theory, which require the assumption that the wall is rigid and unyielding. This means that the same load would be applied for the active and passive earth pressure cases. The assumption of an unyielding wall would be conservative for the active earth pressure case but may be unconservative for the passive earth pressure case, depending on the specific application.

If the retaining structure is expected to yield or move sufficiently to develop active conditions, then 75% of the load calculated using the following methods can be used. This value will be approximately halfway between the pressures expected for yielding and unyielding walls, and thus, should still be conservative.

It is prudent to include surface loads on the backfill of retaining structures in urban construction since it may not be possible to determine future loads. Construction materials can sometimes be stockpiled on the ground surface near the top of walls, or loads applied by construction equipment may be present. Sometimes, building codes require a specified minimum distributed load be applied to the top of the retaining structure backfill for design calculations.
key_points: Five load types are addressed: uniform surcharge, rectangular surface load, point load, line load parallel to wall, and line load perpendicular to wall.
Solutions are based on elastic theory assuming a rigid, unyielding wall — conservative for active case, potentially unconservative for passive case.
When active conditions develop (wall yields sufficiently), 75% of the elastically computed load may be used as a conservative approximation.
Urban construction should always account for surface loads due to uncertain future loads, stockpiled materials, and construction equipment.
Building codes may require a specified minimum distributed load to be applied to retaining structure backfill in design.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever surface loads (surcharge, point, or line loads) are present behind a retaining structure and must be included in lateral earth pressure design.

sections.title: Surcharge Loading
sections.summary: Covers the treatment of a uniform surcharge load (q) of large lateral extent applied behind a retaining structure. In Rankine theory, q is added directly to the vertical effective stress at all depths. In the Coulomb method, q multiplies the horizontal length of the top boundary of the soil wedge to obtain the weight increment.
sections.body: In many cases, loads behind retaining structures are idealized as a uniform surcharge or uniformly loaded (q) area with large extent compared to the wall size. A surcharge is relatively easy to accommodate in Rankine earth pressure theory because q can directly be added to the vertical effective stress term for all depths. In the Coulomb method, the increase in the weight of the soil wedge can be calculated by multiplying q by the horizontal length of the top boundary of the wedge.
key_points: Uniform surcharge q has large lateral extent relative to wall height and is the simplest surface load case.
In Rankine theory, q is added directly to the vertical effective stress at every depth, increasing lateral pressure uniformly.
In the Coulomb wedge method, the wedge weight increment equals q multiplied by the horizontal length of the wedge's top boundary.
sections.applicability: Applies when the surface load behind a retaining structure can be idealized as a uniform pressure of large lateral extent relative to the wall.

sections.title: Uniform Rectangular Surface Load
sections.summary: Addresses a rectangular uniform load of limited extent (length L along wall, width B perpendicular) on wall backfill. Influence factors from Figure 4-17 give horizontal stress at the corner of the loaded area; superposition is used to find stress at the midpoint. A 300 psf surcharge over 20–30 ft from the wall is a common design assumption for construction equipment and materials.
sections.body:
The wall backfill may support a rectangular uniform load that extends a limited distance (L) along the wall and extends a distance (B) perpendicular to the wall. The additional horizontal stress applied to the wall at the corner of this load can be calculated using the influence factors in Figure 4-17. The surcharge load, q, is expressed in units of stress or pressure. The highest horizontal stress will be applied to the wall at the midpoint of the loaded area, corresponding to a load width of L/2. Because the chart determines the pressure at the corner of the loaded area, the principle of superposition (NAVFAC DM-7.1 Chapter 4) should be used to determine the horizontal stress at the midpoint.

For design purposes, it is common to consider a distributed surface load surcharge on the order of 300 psf to account for storage of construction materials and equipment. This surcharge is usually applied within a rather limited work area of about 20 feet to 30 feet from the wall and can also be used to account for concentrated loads from heavy equipment (concrete trucks, cranes, etc.) located more than about 20 feet away. If such equipment is anticipated within a few feet of the wall, it must be accounted for separately using the methods described in the following sections.
key_points: Rectangular load of limited extent is characterized by length L along the wall and width B perpendicular to the wall.
Figure 4-17 influence factors give horizontal stress at the corner of the loaded area on an unyielding wall.
Superposition (per NAVFAC DM-7.1 Ch. 4) is required to obtain the maximum stress at the midpoint of the loaded area (using L/2).
A 300 psf surcharge over 20–30 ft from the wall is a common design assumption for construction materials and equipment.
Heavy equipment within a few feet of the wall must be analyzed separately as point or line loads.
figures: Figure 4-17 Lateral Pressure on an Unyielding Wall at the Corner of a Uniform Rectangular Surface Load
sections.applicability: Applies when backfill behind a retaining wall supports a rectangular uniform load of limited lateral extent, such as a construction staging area or material stockpile.

sections.title: Point Load
sections.summary: Covers the modified elastic solution for lateral pressure and resultant horizontal force (PH) on a retaining wall from a point load (QP) on the backfill, as shown in Figure 4-18. Influence curves are parameterized by m (distance to load divided by wall height). For m ≤ 0.4 a single curve applies; for m > 0.4 the correct curve must be selected. PH location (y from ground) is read from an inset table.
sections.body:
A point load on the backfill of a retaining structure might be the force applied by an outrigger of a crane or other similar condition where a force is applied over a small area. Sometimes, the loads caused by construction traffic are modeled assuming that the tire contact positions are point loads, and the principle of superposition is applied to calculate the load applied by all of the tires.

The modified elastic solution for the pressure distribution and the horizontal resultant force (PH) from a point load (Qp) is shown in Figure 4-18. Since a point load is limited in lateral extent, the force applied to the wall is greatest at the minimum perpendicular distance from the point load to the wall.

The individual curves shown on the influence chart are for different values of m, which is the distance to the load divided by the height of the wall. For values of m ≤ 0.4, the solution is not closely dependent on m, and the same influence curve can be used for all values of m ≤ 0.4. For values of m > 0.4, the proper influence curve should be used corresponding to the value of m.

The value of the resultant force (PH) can be estimated as a function of m from the inset table on the influence chart. The point of application of PH, located a vertical distance (y) from the ground level on the front of the wall, can be calculated using the table for different values of m. The value of PH is the maximum force per unit length of wall caused by QP, rather than the total horizontal load for the entire length of wall. Thus, PH occurs at the point where θ is zero degrees.

The horizontal variation of pressure (σHθ) can be calculated from the maximum pressure exerted by the point load (σH) for a given depth based on the angle (θ) between a horizontal line drawn from the point load to the wall and a line drawn from the point load to the point on the wall where σHθ is to be calculated.
key_points: Point loads represent crane outriggers, tire contact areas, or other small-footprint loads; superposition handles multiple tires.
Figure 4-18 provides modified elastic influence curves for horizontal pressure distribution and resultant PH as a function of m = (distance to load) / (wall height).
For m ≤ 0.4, influence is nearly independent of m; a single curve applies. For m > 0.4, the specific m curve must be used.
PH is the maximum force per unit length of wall (not total wall force) and occurs directly opposite the point load (θ = 0°).
Lateral variation of pressure σHθ is determined from the maximum pressure σH and the angle θ from the normal to the wall through the load point.
figures: Figure 4-18 Horizontal Pressure and Resultant Force for a Single Point Load Applied at the Surface of the Backfill
sections.applicability: Applies when a concentrated force (crane outrigger, construction equipment tire, etc.) is applied over a small area on the backfill surface behind a retaining wall.

sections.title: Line Load Parallel to the Structure
sections.summary: Covers lateral pressure on a retaining wall from a line load (QL, force per unit length) oriented parallel to the wall, representing a strip footing or similar infinite-length loading. Figure 4-19 provides influence factors parameterized by m. For m ≤ 0.4 the m = 0.4 curve is used; for m > 0.4 the chart or formula in Figure 4-19 is applied. Pressures are uniform along the wall length.
sections.body:
A line load on the backfill of a retaining structure can be used to represent a strip footing from a structure or other long, narrow loading. Line loads (QL) are considered to be as long as the retaining wall, and the loads are expressed as a force per distance. Since line loads are considered numerically to be of infinite length, the calculated pressures do not vary along the length of the retaining structure.

Similar to the equations for a point load, the influence factors do not vary considerably for values of m ≤ 0.4, and the curve shown for m = 0.4 can be used for m values less than 0.4 as well. For values of m > 0.4, the influence value can be read off of the chart if the correct value of m is available, or it can be calculated from the formula indicated in Figure 4-19.
key_points: Line loads (QL) run parallel to and the full length of the retaining wall; pressures are uniform along the wall length.
Line loads represent strip footings or similar long, narrow loading conditions; expressed as force per unit length.
Figure 4-19 provides influence factors; for m ≤ 0.4 use the m = 0.4 curve, for m > 0.4 use the chart or the formula in Figure 4-19.
The infinite-length assumption means lateral pressure does not vary along the wall, simplifying design to a 2D problem.
figures: Figure 4-19 Horizontal Pressure and Resultant Force for Line Load Applied at the Surface of the Backfill Parallel to the Retaining Structure
sections.applicability: Applies when a long, narrow load such as a strip footing runs parallel to a retaining wall and must be included in lateral earth pressure design.

sections.title: Line Load Perpendicular to the Structure
sections.summary: Covers lateral pressure on a retaining wall from a line load (Q) oriented perpendicular to the wall, expressed as force per unit length. Maximum pressure occurs at the intersection of the load line and the wall and decreases in both directions along the wall. Figure 4-20 defines geometry and gives the general solution form; Figure 4-21 provides influence factors for specific cases.
sections.body:
Figure 4-20 and Figure 4-21 show the geometry for a line load (Q) oriented perpendicular to the structure, expressed as a force per unit length. The maximum pressure is applied to the wall at the perpendicular intersection of the line load and the wall. The pressure decreases along the wall in each direction from this point.

Figure 4-20 shows the general form of the solution for a line load parallel to the wall along with the geometric definitions. Figure 4-21 provides influence factors for specific situations.
key_points: A line load perpendicular to the wall produces maximum lateral pressure directly at the wall intersection and decreases bilaterally along the wall.
Load Q is expressed as force per unit length and is oriented perpendicular to the retaining structure.
Figure 4-20 presents geometry definitions and the general solution form for this loading configuration.
Figure 4-21 provides influence factors for specific cases of perpendicular line loads.
figures: Figure 4-20 General form of the solution for a line load perpendicular to the wall with geometric definitions
Figure 4-21 Influence factors for line load perpendicular to the retaining structure
sections.applicability: Applies when a line load runs perpendicular to a retaining wall (e.g., a strip footing or roadway load approaching the wall at a right angle) and lateral pressures along the wall must be determined.

sections.title: Earth Pressures Due to Compaction
sections.summary: Covers the two types of loads a compactor imposes on a retaining wall — transient loads and locked-in horizontal stresses — and provides methods to calculate locked-in compaction pressures using charts (Figures 4-22 to 4-24) and correction factor tables (Tables 4-4 to 4-6) from Duncan et al. (1991) for rollers, vibratory plates, and rammer plates.
sections.body:
The operation of a compactor near a retaining structure can impose two types of loads on the wall. First, a transient load can be applied due to the weight of the compactor and the force applied at the ground surface. Second, horizontal stress can be "locked-in" due to the compaction process, and this increased pressure can remain after the compactor is removed.

The "locked-in" horizontal pressures from compaction can be calculated using tables and figures from Duncan et al. (1991). In Figure 4-22 to Figure 4-24, the earth pressures due to compaction by rollers are shown by the solid and single-dashed lines. The at-rest earth pressures are shown for comparison using dash-dot lines. The charts were developed from experimental data on rollers, plate compactors, and rammer plates operating 0 to 0.5 feet from the wall. The lift thickness varied from 0.33 to 0.5 feet and the backfill material had a friction angle of 35 degrees. For compaction conditions that vary from these assumptions, correction factors for the earth pressure are given in Table 4-4 to Table 4-6.

The force imparted by the specific compactor can be found by consulting the manufacturer's information. Duncan et al. (1991) summarized the compactor specifications for many small compactors at the time of publication of the paper. The specifications for current compactors should be checked prior to using these tables and figures.
key_points: Compactors impose two load types on retaining walls: (1) transient loads from compactor weight/force, and (2) residual 'locked-in' horizontal stresses that persist after compactor removal.
Locked-in compaction pressures are calculated using charts from Duncan et al. (1991) — Figures 4-22 to 4-24 — covering rollers, vibratory plates, and rammer plates.
Base charts assume compactor operating 0–0.5 ft from wall, lift thickness 0.33–0.5 ft, and backfill friction angle φ′ = 35°; deviations require correction factors.
Correction factors for distance from wall, lift thickness, equipment dimensions, and friction angle are provided in Tables 4-4 through 4-6 as depth-dependent multipliers at z = 2, 4, 8, and 16 ft.
Compactor force data must be obtained from manufacturer specifications; Duncan et al. (1991) data on small compactors may be outdated and should be verified for current equipment.
Discussions and closure to Duncan et al. (1991) contain important corrections that are reflected in the figures and tables included in this UFC.

sections.title: Seismic Earth Pressures on Retaining Structures
sections.summary: Introduces the framework for evaluating seismic earth pressures on retaining structures per FEMA 2009 NEHRP provisions. Covers the two major categories of retaining walls (yielding and nonyielding), defines seismic ground acceleration parameters (kv, kh), and notes that waterfront structures have historically performed poorly under earthquake loading.
sections.body:
Earthquakes can increase the loading on retaining structures. In the past, waterfront structures have performed poorly under earthquake loading (FEMA 2009). The methods for calculating the effects of seismic loading are rapidly evolving. The procedures presented in this section are very basic and are based on the 2009 edition of the NEHRP Recommended Seismic Provisions (FEMA 2009). Earthquake assessment of retaining structure is an evolving topic, and the users of this manual are encouraged to seek out the most recent design guidance. Seismic effects are quantified in terms of the vertical ground acceleration (kv) and horizontal ground acceleration (kh), both in units of gravity.

Retaining structures are separated into two major categories: (1) yielding walls that are free to rotate or laterally translate, and (2) nonyielding walls, such as basement walls that are restrained on the top and bottom.
key_points: Seismic loading is quantified by vertical (kv) and horizontal (kh) ground accelerations in units of gravity.
Waterfront retaining structures have historically performed poorly under earthquake loading.
Retaining walls are classified as either yielding (free to rotate/translate) or nonyielding (restrained top and bottom).
Procedures are based on FEMA 2009 NEHRP Recommended Seismic Provisions; users should seek current guidance as methods evolve.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating seismic earth pressure effects on any retaining structure.

sections.title: Yielding Walls
sections.summary: Covers the Mononobe-Okabe (M-O) seismic coefficient method for yielding retaining walls, providing equations for the seismic active earth pressure coefficient (KAE) and seismic earth force (PAE). Also presents the Seed and Whitman (1970) simplified decomposition into static and dynamic components, with dynamic force acting at 0.6H. Includes application notes for sloped backfill and battered walls, and limitations of the M-O method.
sections.body:
The assessment of yielding walls is based on the Coulomb earth pressure theory presented earlier in this chapter. The wall movement is assumed to be sufficient to allow an active earth pressure condition to develop. The framework that has been adopted for analysis is the Mononobe-Okabe (M-O) seismic coefficient analysis (Mononobe and Matsuo 1929; Okabe 1924).

The seismic active earth pressure coefficient (KAE) considers the normal factors in a Coulomb analysis (i.e., soil strength, backfill slope, interface friction angle, slope of wall face) and also the horizontal and vertical ground acceleration. KAE can be calculated by Eq. 4-15.

The basic equation for calculating the seismic earth pressure assumes that the backfill material is a cohesionless soil and that the phreatic surface is below the base of the wall. With these assumptions, the seismic earth force is given by Eq. 4-16.

Seed and Whitman (1970) provide a simplified application of Equation 4-16 by separating the total applied earth pressure force (PAE) into static (PA) and dynamic (ΔPAE) components. The static component is calculated as described in Section 4-3. For the case of a horizontal backfill, vertical wall face, and no wall friction, the dynamic component is calculated by Eq. 4-17.

The dynamic component of the earth pressure force is assumed to act at 0.6H above the wall base. This simplified approach is limited to cases where the backfill is horizontal and the wall height is less than 20 feet. An example for calculating the static and dynamic forces acting on a wall is shown in Figure 4-25.

The M-O procedure can also be applied for conditions where the backfill is not horizontal and the wall has a batter. The combined active earth pressure force can be calculated using Equation 4-16. If separate values of the static and dynamic earth pressure forces are desired, the conventional static active earth pressure force, PA, can be calculated using KA determined from the values of β and θ. The dynamic component, ΔPAE, can be calculated by subtracting PA from PAE.

The resultant force for this method can vary in its location depending on wall movement, ground acceleration, and wall batter. For practical purposes, it may be applied at 0.6H above the base of the wall. An example using the M-O method for a wall having a sloping backfill and face is shown in Figure 4-26.

The M-O method should not be used for site conditions where there are high ground accelerations and complex soil backfill conditions. For more complex conditions, evaluation of ground motions is often required, and numerical methods assessing wall displacements are employed.

If the wall does not move or rotate sufficient to develop active pressure, the actual applied pressure can be much greater than the pressure calculated using the M-O method. If there is uncertainty about the ability of the wall to displace sufficiently, more advanced numerical methods are warranted.
key_points: M-O method (Mononobe-Okabe) extends Coulomb earth pressure theory to include seismic acceleration coefficients kh and kv.
KAE (Eq. 4-15) accounts for soil friction angle, backfill slope, wall slope, interface friction angle, and seismic angle ψ = tan⁻¹(kh/(1−kv)).
Total seismic earth force PAE (Eq. 4-16) assumes cohesionless backfill with phreatic surface below wall base.
Seed and Whitman simplified approach (Eq. 4-17) separates PAE into static and dynamic components; dynamic force acts at 0.6H above base.
Simplified Seed-Whitman approach is limited to horizontal backfill and wall heights < 20 ft.
M-O method is not appropriate for high ground accelerations or complex backfill conditions; numerical methods should be used instead.
If wall cannot displace sufficiently for active pressure to develop, actual pressures may far exceed M-O predictions.

equations.description: Seismic active earth pressure coefficient KAE as a function of backfill friction angle φ', backfill slope β, wall slope θ, interface friction angle δ, and seismic angle ψ = tan⁻¹(kh/(1−kv)).
Total seismic active earth pressure force PAE = (1−kv)/2 · γ · H² · KAE, for cohesionless backfill with phreatic surface below wall base.
Dynamic earth pressure force component ΔPAE = (3/8) · kh · γ · H², for horizontal backfill, vertical wall face, no wall friction, and wall height < 20 ft (Seed and Whitman 1970 simplification).
