Figure 4-26 Example of M-O Method for a Retaining Wall Having a Sloping Face and a Sloping Backfill
sections.applicability: Applies to retaining walls that are free to rotate or laterally translate, allowing active earth pressure conditions to develop under seismic loading.

sections.title: Nonyielding Walls
sections.summary: Covers seismic earth pressure calculation for nonyielding walls (e.g., basement walls, rigid walls on rock) that cannot develop active earth pressures. Presents Wood (1973) simplified formula for the incremental seismic earth pressure force ΔPE (Eq. 4-18), which is added to static pressure. Notes that more advanced solutions accounting for inertial and kinematic soil-structure interaction effects also exist.
sections.body:
Walls that are unable to develop seismic active earth pressures are considered to be nonyielding walls. Basement walls are often used as a practical example of a nonyielding wall. Very rigid walls founded on rock can classify as nonyielding walls. Wood (1973) developed a simplified approach to calculate an increase in the earth pressure force (ΔPE) for nonyielding walls during seismic events. This force would be added to the existing static pressure to determine the total applied force. The earth pressure force can be calculated by Eq. 4-18.

The point of application of ΔPE is normally assumed to be at 0.6H above the base of the wall. Other solutions for nonyielding walls include inertial effects and kinematic soil-structure interaction effects.
key_points: Nonyielding walls (e.g., basement walls, walls on rock) cannot develop seismic active pressures, so M-O method is not applicable.
Wood (1973) simplified formula gives incremental seismic earth pressure force ΔPE = kh · γ · H² (Eq. 4-18), added to existing static pressure.
The incremental seismic force ΔPE is applied at 0.6H above the wall base.
More advanced solutions accounting for inertial effects and kinematic soil-structure interaction exist for nonyielding walls.

equations.description: Incremental seismic earth pressure force for nonyielding walls: ΔPE = kh · γ · H² (Wood 1973), added to static pressure to obtain total applied force.

sections.applicability: Applies to walls restrained against rotation and translation (nonyielding walls) that cannot develop seismic active earth pressures during seismic events.

sections.title: Dynamic Water Pressure
sections.summary: Addresses the change in water pressure on retaining walls due to seismic loading for saturated backfill conditions. Separates calculation approaches by soil hydraulic conductivity, noting that methods for partially submerged conditions are available in Kramer (1996) and Matsuzawa et al. (1985). Subsections cover high and (implicitly) low hydraulic conductivity soils.
sections.body: Seismic loading also changes the water pressure applied to walls. The solutions presented below assume that the backfill is saturated. Methods for partially submerged conditions can be found in Kramer (1996) and Matsuzawa et al. (1985). Calculation approaches can be separated by the hydraulic conductivity of the soil.
key_points: Seismic loading changes water pressure on retaining walls in addition to earth pressure.
Solutions assume saturated backfill; partially submerged conditions require methods from Kramer (1996) or Matsuzawa et al. (1985).
Approach is divided by soil hydraulic conductivity (high vs. low permeability soils).
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating dynamic water pressure effects on retaining walls with saturated backfill under seismic loading.

sections.title: High Hydraulic Conductivity Soils
sections.summary: Provides the equation for hydrodynamic water pressure (pw) on retaining walls for soils with hydraulic conductivity greater than ~10⁻³ cm/s, where pore water acts independently of the soil skeleton. The pressure varies with depth below the phreatic surface and total water depth behind the wall. Uses Eq. 4-19 to compute pw as a function of kh, γw, z, and H.
sections.body:
For soil with hydraulic conductivity greater than about 10⁻³ cm/s, the water in the voids will act independently of the soil and will impart a hydrodynamic water pressure (pw) that can be calculated as Eq. 4-19.

where:
γw = unit weight of water,
z = depth below the phreatic surface, and
H = total depth of water behind the wall.
key_points: Applies to soils with hydraulic conductivity > ~10⁻³ cm/s (e.g., gravels, coarse sands).
In high-permeability soils, pore water acts independently of the soil skeleton during seismic shaking.
Hydrodynamic water pressure pw = 0.875 · kh · γw · √(H·z) (Eq. 4-19), varying with depth z below the phreatic surface and total water depth H.

equations.description: Hydrodynamic water pressure for high hydraulic conductivity soils (k > 10⁻³ cm/s): pw = 0.875 · kh · γw · √(H·z), where γw is unit weight of water, z is depth below phreatic surface, and H is total water depth behind the wall.

sections.applicability: Applies to retaining walls with saturated backfill of high hydraulic conductivity (> ~10⁻³ cm/s) under seismic loading.

sections.title: Rigid Gravity Retaining Structures
sections.summary: Introduces the two fundamental categories of retaining structures—rigid gravity and flexible—and focuses on rigid walls. Covers the monolithic displacement behavior of rigid walls, construction process, and typical examples (concrete gravity, cantilever, counterfort, buttress, gabion). Directs the reader to subsequent subsections for design calculations and drainage.
sections.body:
The preceding sections provide the theories for calculating earth and water pressures on retaining structures. A key element in the development of earth pressures is the wall movement or displacement. For design, retaining structures are divided into two basic categories: (1) rigid gravity structures and (2) flexible structures. Alternative forms of gravity structure are presented in Section 4-6. The design of flexible walls is discussed in Section 4-7.

Rigid retaining walls are structures that displace (translation or rotation) monolithically, and for the most part, they develop their lateral resistance from their own weight and the weight of overlying soil. The construction process for rigid walls typically involves construction of the wall followed by the placement of backfill. Examples of rigid retaining structures are concrete gravity walls, concrete cantilever walls, counterfort walls, buttress walls, and gabion walls. The design of rigid retaining structures is discussed in this section.
key_points: Rigid gravity walls displace monolithically (translation or rotation) and resist lateral loads via self-weight and overlying soil weight.
Construction sequence: wall is built first, then backfill is placed.
Examples include concrete gravity, cantilever, counterfort, buttress, and gabion walls.
Four failure modes are evaluated: overturning, sliding, bearing capacity/settlement, and global stability.
Passive pressure on the front of the wall is typically ignored because the displacement needed to mobilize it is too large.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever a rigid gravity retaining structure is being designed or analyzed for lateral earth pressure resistance.

sections.title: Design Calculations for Rigid Retaining Walls
sections.summary: Describes the overall framework for designing rigid retaining walls using free-body diagrams. Identifies the four failure modes to be checked—overturning, sliding, bearing capacity/settlement, and global stability—and explains why passive pressure on the wall toe is typically ignored in stability assessments.
sections.body:
Examples of four rigid retaining walls are shown in Figure 4-27. The pressures acting on the face of rigid walls follow the theory, presented earlier in this chapter, that depends on the displacement or rotation of the wall. Once the earth and water pressures are determined, the forces and pressures acting on the other parts of the wall are assessed so that an entire free-body diagram can be constructed. With a knowledge of the FBD, a variety of modes of failure can be assessed. Figure 4-27 summarizes the calculations for the following modes of failure:
1) Overturning,
2) Sliding,
3) Bearing capacity and settlement, and
4) Global or overall stability.

Passive forces are indicated above the toe of the retaining walls in Figure 4-27. However, the passive pressure on the front of the wall is typically ignored when assessing the stability. As shown in Figure 4-1, there is a marked difference in displacement required for developing passive pressure as compared to active pressure. By the time that full passive pressure has been developed, the wall displacement would be too great for the performance to be considered satisfactory. Also, the soil in front of the wall might be excavated at a later date, so relying on passive pressure often is not warranted.
key_points: Full free-body diagram must be constructed before assessing failure modes.
Four failure modes: overturning, sliding, bearing capacity/settlement, global stability.
Passive pressure at the toe is typically ignored—full mobilization requires excessive wall displacement.
Soil in front of the wall may be excavated later, making passive resistance unreliable.
sections.applicability: Applies to all rigid retaining wall designs requiring a systematic stability assessment across multiple failure modes.

sections.title: Pressure Distribution at the Base of Walls
sections.summary: Defines how to calculate and interpret the pressure distribution at the base of a rigid retaining wall. Covers the resultant normal force R, eccentricity e, and provides equations for maximum and minimum bearing pressures under trapezoidal and triangular distributions, as well as a simplified uniform pressure approach when R falls outside the middle third.
sections.body:
The pressure distribution acting on the base of retaining walls impacts the stability assessment for different failure modes. Using the equations for force equilibrium, the magnitude of the resultant normal force (R) and the shear force (T) can be determined. The location of R can be determined from moment equilibrium about the toe of the wall. The distance that R acts from the centerline or midpoint of the base of the wall is defined as the eccentricity, e. Figure 4-27 provides the method for calculating the resultant location and eccentricity.

Knowledge of the magnitude and position of R allows the pressure distribution on the bottom of the wall to be calculated. Theoretically, the shape of pressure distribution is either triangular or trapezoidal as shown in Figure 4-28. If the resultant acts precisely at the one-third point of the base, a triangular pressure distribution results, with the full base of the wall under compression. If the resultant acts within the middle third of the base, a trapezoidal distribution results, and the maximum pressure, qmax, acting at the toe is given by Equation 4-23. The resultant of the pressure distribution acts at the centroid of the pressure diagram. The minimum pressure, qmin, acting on the heel side of the trapezoidal pressure distribution that provides the correct location of the resultant (R) can be calculated by Equation 4-24.

If the resultant is located outside of the middle third of the base, the maximum stress can be calculated by Equation 4-25, where x0 = B/2 – e = horizontal distance between R and the toe. When the resultant is outside of the middle third of the base, only a portion of the base is under compression. The amount of base under compression, Be, can be calculated by Equation 4-26.

As shown at the bottom of Figure 4-28, the pressure distribution can be simplified by assuming that the pressure acts uniformly over a width of 2·x0. If the pressure distribution is assumed to be uniform, its magnitude is given by Equation 4-27. For the simplified uniform distribution of pressure, the amount of the base that is under compression is given by Equation 4-28.
key_points: Eccentricity e is the distance R acts from the base centerline; determined by moment equilibrium about the toe.
Resultant within middle third → trapezoidal pressure distribution; at one-third point → triangular distribution.
qmax (toe) = R/B + 6Re/B²; qmin (heel) = R/B − 6Re/B² for trapezoidal case.
Resultant outside middle third: only portion Be = 3x0 of base is in compression; qmax = R/(2·x0·1).
Simplified uniform pressure over width 2x0 may be used when soil is ductile: Be = 2x0.
Pressure distribution choice affects bearing capacity check—triangular/trapezoidal required for brittle materials.

equations.description: Maximum bearing pressure qmax at the toe for trapezoidal distribution when resultant is within middle third: qmax = R/B + 6Re/B²
Minimum bearing pressure qmin at the heel for trapezoidal distribution: qmin = R/B − 6Re/B²
Maximum bearing pressure qmax when resultant is outside middle third: qmax = R / (2·x0), where x0 = B/2 − e
Length of base under compression when resultant is outside middle third: Be = 3·x0
Maximum pressure under simplified uniform distribution: qmax = R / (2·x0)
Effective base width under compression for simplified uniform distribution: Be = 2·x0

sections.applicability: Applies when calculating base pressure distributions for rigid retaining walls to support bearing capacity, overturning, and sliding checks.

sections.title: Overturning
sections.summary: Describes two methods for checking overturning stability of rigid retaining walls: (1) factor of safety FOT ≥ 1.5 defined as restoring moment divided by overturning moment, and (2) resultant location check—middle third of base for soil-founded walls, middle half for rock-founded walls. Notes wider LRFD thresholds when factored loads are used.
sections.body:
The stability of the wall for the failure mode of overturning can be determined by defining a factor of safety equal to the restoring moment divided by the overturning moment. The factor of safety, FOT, should be greater than or equal to 1.5.

An alternative method is to examine the location of the resultant, R, relative to the width of the base of the wall. If R is in the middle one-third of the base for walls founded on soil, the wall is considered safe. For walls founded on rock, R should be located in the middle one-half of the base for the wall to be considered safe.

Note: If LRFD techniques are used for design, there are wider thresholds for the location of the resultant force if factored loads are used.
key_points: FOT = restoring moment / overturning moment; minimum FOT = 1.5.
Alternative check: R must fall within middle third of base for soil-founded walls.
For rock-founded walls, R must fall within middle half of base.
LRFD design allows wider resultant location thresholds when factored loads are applied.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing overturning stability of rigid gravity retaining walls founded on either soil or rock.

sections.title: Sliding
sections.summary: Covers the calculation of factor of safety against sliding (FSL ≥ 1.5) for rigid retaining walls, using horizontal force equilibrium. Addresses base friction, adhesion, passive resistance, layered bearing materials, and the use of a wall key to increase sliding resistance. Explains when FSL must be raised to 2.0.
sections.body:
The stability of the wall for the failure mode of sliding is normally determined by using horizontal force equilibrium. The factor of safety against sliding, FSL, is the ratio of the resisting force to the horizontal earth pressure force. The resisting force is a combination of the frictional resistance at the base of the wall and the adhesion between the base of the wall and the soil foundation. For sliding resistance on fine-grained soils, the adhesion should be multiplied by the effective width of the base (Be) found using the uniform bearing pressure method. The factor of safety should be greater than or equal to 1.5. The parameters used to calculate FSL are shown on Figure 4-27. If passive resistance is included, the minimum FSL should be increased to 2.0. Minimum FSL may also need to be increased when base adhesion is included in the resistance.

In some cases, a layer of coarse-grained soil may be placed below the wall as a bearing material. Sliding should be checked at two locations. The shear resistance, T, should be taken as the lowest of (1) the resistance at the interface between the base of the wall and the bearing material and (2) the resistance within the clay using the full undrained shear strength.

If stability against sliding is an issue, gravity retaining walls can be designed with a key to increase the sliding resistance by adding a passive resistance component. Figure 4-29 shows an outline of the analysis method to accommodate a wall base with a key. Note that the passive pressure is applied only along the depth of the key and not along the entire burial depth of the wall. It is also prudent to consider some amount of future excavation in front of the wall that would reduce passive resistance.
key_points: FSL = resisting force / horizontal earth pressure force; minimum FSL = 1.5.
Resisting force = base friction + base-soil adhesion; adhesion multiplied by effective base width Be for fine-grained soils.
If passive resistance is included, minimum FSL increases to 2.0.
For layered bearing materials, check sliding at both the wall-bearing material interface and within the clay layer.
A wall key can be added to increase passive resistance; passive pressure applies only over key depth, not full burial depth.
Future excavation in front of the wall should be anticipated, reducing passive resistance.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating sliding stability of rigid retaining walls, particularly where soil conditions or geometry make sliding a governing failure mode.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity and Settlement
sections.summary: Explains how to assess bearing capacity and settlement beneath rigid retaining walls. The wall base is treated as a strip footing with eccentric inclined loading (Chapter 5). Required factor of safety is 2.5–3. Discusses the choice between uniform vs. triangular/trapezoidal pressure distributions and the destabilizing effect of differential settlement between wall and backfill.
sections.body:
The bearing capacity of the soil below a retaining wall is calculated by assuming the wall acts as a conventional strip footing with eccentric, inclined loading, which is discussed in Chapter 5. The depth of embedment is equal to the depth on the toe side of the wall.

The bearing capacity should be compared to the maximum bearing pressure calculated as shown in Figure 4-28. A factor of safety of 2.5 to 3 is typically appropriate. A uniform pressure distribution can be used to determine qmax if the soil below the wall is relatively ductile. For more brittle materials, such as rock and sensitive clays, the triangular or trapezoidal pressure distribution should be used to find qmax. Because load inclination affects bearing capacity, the factor of safety against bearing capacity failure and sliding are often closely related.

Settlement of retaining walls can be an important factor in overall stability. For the examples shown in Figure 4-27, the backfill places a downward pressure on the retaining wall. This pressure increases the contact stress at the base of the wall, thus increasing the sliding resistance. If the wall settles considerably more than the backfill, then the relative movement between the wall and backfill can be reversed, and the vertical pressure can act up instead of down. This is a destabilizing force on the wall since it decreases the resistance to sliding.

Settlement analyses can be performed using the procedures outlined in Chapter 5 of DM 7.1. Settlement should consider net changes in stress by comparing the conditions before and after the wall was constructed.
key_points: Wall base treated as a strip footing with eccentric, inclined loading; embedment depth taken at the toe side.
Factor of safety against bearing capacity failure: 2.5 to 3.
Use uniform qmax for ductile soils; use triangular/trapezoidal qmax for brittle materials (rock, sensitive clays).
Bearing capacity FS and sliding FS are closely related because load inclination affects both.
Excessive wall settlement relative to backfill reverses vertical pressure, reducing sliding resistance (destabilizing).
Settlement analysis follows DM 7.1 Chapter 5; use net stress changes before vs. after construction.
sections.applicability: Applies when checking bearing capacity and settlement beneath rigid retaining walls founded on soil or rock.

sections.title: Overall or Global Stability
sections.summary: Addresses global (overall) stability of rigid retaining walls using slope stability analysis methods. The failure mechanism involves slip surfaces passing through the backfill and wall mass. Directs the designer to slope stability procedures in DM 7.1 Chapter 7.
sections.body: Overall or global stability is assessed using the same tools employed for slope stability analysis. This mechanism of failure considers slip surfaces that extend from the back of the wall to the front of the wall, and the slide mass contains the wall and backfill. Slope stability is discussed in Chapter 7 of DM 7.1.
key_points: Global stability uses slope stability analysis methods (DM 7.1 Chapter 7).
Slip surfaces extend from the back to the front of the wall, encompassing the entire wall and backfill mass.
This failure mode is distinct from sliding, overturning, and bearing capacity failures.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing the overall (global) stability of a rigid retaining wall system, especially where soft or layered foundation soils are present.

sections.title: Design of Low Walls
sections.summary: Provides a simplified design approach for low retaining walls (under 12 feet tall) using equivalent fluid pressures when failure consequences are not significant. References Figure 4-30 for equivalent fluid unit weights by USCS soil type and notes the broken backslope accommodation. Cautions that chart origins are unclear and results should be verified by other methods.
sections.body:
For low retaining walls (less than 12 feet tall), the retaining wall loads can be calculated based on equivalent fluid pressures, provided the consequences of failure are not significant. Figure 4-30 provides a method for determining the loads on low retaining walls for three different soil categories based on the Unified Soil Classification System. This method accommodates a broken backslope, in which the backslope levels are relatively close to the wall. The equivalent fluid unit weights can be used to calculate horizontal and vertical forces applied to the wall.

Figure 4-30 is based on equivalent fluid pressures associated with the different soil types listed above, and similar charts are found in several geotechnical textbooks. However, the specific details on how these charts were created are unclear. If these charts are used, it is prudent to check the results using other methods.
key_points: Simplified equivalent fluid pressure method applicable only to walls < 12 ft tall and where failure consequences are not significant.
Equivalent fluid unit weights are categorized by USCS soil type (three categories) per Figure 4-30.
Method accommodates a broken backslope geometry.
Chart origins are unclear; results should always be verified with other analytical methods.
sections.applicability: Applies to low retaining walls (less than 12 feet tall) where simplified load estimation is acceptable and failure consequences are limited.

sections.title: Drainage Behind Rigid Walls
sections.summary: Explains the critical importance of drainage systems behind rigid retaining structures. Describes how a phreatic surface in backfill reduces effective stress but increases total lateral force, making water pressure a common cause of retaining wall failures. Lists three design criteria for drainage systems and references Figure 4-31 for example drainage and filter configurations.
sections.body:
Water should not be allowed to pond behind retaining structures or within the backfill, if at all possible. The presence of a phreatic surface in the wall backfill decreases the effective stress in the soil, so the earth pressure is reduced. However, as discussed in Section 4-4.1, the water itself applies a pressure to the wall, and the net result is that lateral forces on the wall are increased. Many failures of retaining structures are due to unanticipated or unmitigated water pressures.

Drainage systems should be incorporated into the design of retaining structures if there is a potential for water pressures to act on the wall. The drainage system design should satisfy several criteria:
1) An elevated water table should not be present behind the wall, even in the case of large rainfall events.
2) Any water that finds its way to the backfill should be safely conveyed away from the wall. The water should be drained laterally down the wall to a safe exit or through weep holes in the face of the wall.
3) The drainage system should not allow erosion of the backfill materials or migrations of fines within the backfill. This may require the use of a graded filter or geosynthetic filter fabric.

Examples of drainage and filter systems that can be incorporated into rigid wall design are shown in Figure 4-31.
key_points: Phreatic surface in backfill reduces effective stress but net lateral force on wall increases due to water pressure—a common failure cause.
Drainage systems must prevent elevated water table behind the wall even during large storms.
Water must be conveyed away from the backfill via lateral drainage to a safe exit or through weep holes.
Drainage systems must prevent erosion and migration of fines; graded filters or geosynthetic filter fabric may be required.
Figure 4-31 provides example drainage and filter system configurations for rigid walls.
sections.applicability: Applies to all rigid retaining wall designs where there is any potential for water to accumulate behind or within the backfill.

sections.title: Alternative Gravity Retaining Structures
sections.summary: Introduces alternative gravity retaining structure types covered in this section: Mechanically Stabilized Earth (MSE) retaining structures, gabion walls, Hesco bastion concertainers, and earth-filled crib and bin walls. Each type is treated as an alternative to conventional rigid retaining walls, with design references and key considerations noted.
key_points: Covers MSE structures, gabion walls, Hesco baskets, and crib/bin walls as alternatives to rigid retaining walls.
All alternatives discussed share the fundamental mass gravity design methodology used for rigid retaining walls.
Design references from FHWA, NAVFAC DM-7.1, and Corps of Engineers standards are cited throughout.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and designing alternative gravity retaining structures in lieu of conventional rigid walls.

sections.title: Mechanical Stabilized Earth (MSE) Retaining Structures
sections.summary: Describes MSE retaining structures as a popular alternative to rigid walls, covering the face-angle criterion distinguishing walls (≥70°) from slopes (<70°), design references (FHWA LRFD and ASD manuals, NAVFAC DM-7.1), and internal/external design requirements including overturning, sliding, bearing capacity, settlement, and global stability.
sections.body:
Mechanically stabilized earth (MSE) retaining structures are a popular alternative to rigid retaining structures. The technology and design methods used for MSE walls and slopes are very similar, and they share the same design manuals from the FHWA. If the face angle of the structure is greater than or equal to 70 degrees, then the structure is considered to be a wall. If the face angle is less than 70 degrees, then the structure is considered to be a slope (FHWA 2009). Walls also have a facing material, while slopes normally do not.
NAVFAC DM-7.1 covers many of the details regarding the internal design of MSE structures in Chapter 7. These details included the backfill materials, reinforcing materials, drainage systems, and the steps for designing MSE structures. These structures must also be designed for overturning, sliding, bearing capacity, settlement, and global stability.
Further discussion of MSE is beyond the scope of this manual. There are several technical reports available from the FHWA that provide design methods for MSE walls and slopes. FHWA (2009) describes Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD) for MSE walls. This manual is considered to be an update for the Allowable Stress Design (ASD) manual, FHWA NHI-00-043 (FHWA 2001).
key_points: Face angle ≥70° classifies the structure as a wall; face angle <70° classifies it as a slope.
Walls require a facing material; slopes normally do not.
NAVFAC DM-7.1 Chapter 7 covers internal design details: backfill, reinforcing, drainage, and design steps.
External design must address overturning, sliding, bearing capacity, settlement, and global stability.
Primary design references: FHWA (2009) LRFD manual and FHWA NHI-00-043 (2001) ASD manual.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing mechanically stabilized earth retaining walls or reinforced slopes as an alternative to rigid retaining structures.

sections.title: Gabion Walls
sections.summary: Details the design and construction of gabion retaining walls, including material specifications (galvanized or PVC-coated wire baskets filled with 4–8 inch stone), design as mass gravity structures per Figure 4-27, batter angle recommendations, interface friction parameters, filter requirements, counterfort guidance for clay slopes, and Hesco bastion concertainers as a related system.
sections.body:
Gabions are compartmented, rectangular containers made of heavily galvanized steel or polyvinylchloride (PVC) coated wire, filled with stone from 4 to 8 inches in size, and are used for control of bank erosion and stabilization as well as earth retaining structures. Design notes for gabion retaining walls are given in Figure 4-32. When the water quality is in doubt (pH > 12 or pH < 6) or where high concentration of organic acid may be present, PVC coated gabions are necessary. At the construction site, the individual gabion units are laced together with wire and filled with stone. Specifications for the gabion baskets are available in the Corps of Engineers CW-02541 (1980).
Gabions are designed as mass gravity structures using the same design procedures as rigid retaining walls that are presented in Figure 4-27. When designing a vertical face wall, it should be battered at an angle of about 6° to keep the resultant force toward the back of the wall. The interface friction angle between the base of a gabion wall and a coarse-grained foundation soil can assumed to be equal to the effective stress friction angle of the foundation. For the back of the wall, the ratio of interface friction to the friction angle of the backfill (δ / φ′) can be set equal to 0.9. Where the retained material is mostly sand, a geosynthetic filter fabric or granular filter is recommended to prevent any erosion of the backfill soil into the gabions. Along all exposed gabion faces, the outer layer of stones should be hand placed to ensure proper alignment, and to achieve a neat, compact, square appearance.
A system of gabion counterforts is recommended when designing gabion structures to retain clay slopes. They should be used as headers and should extend from the front of the wall to a point at least one gabion length beyond the critical slip circle of the bank. Counterforts may be spaced from 13 feet (very soft clay) to 30 feet (stiff clay). A filter is also required on the back of the wall so that clay will not clog the free-draining gabions.
Hesco Bastion Concertainers®, commonly referred to as Hesco baskets, are similar to gabions in that they are wire baskets or cages that are filled with cobbles or other granular soils. Hesco baskets are normally lined with a non-woven geotextile. Common sizes for Hesco baskets are 3 ft x 3 ft x 15 ft and 4 ft x 3 ft x 15 ft. Hesco baskets have been used for a variety of functions in the Armed Forces. They can be used in lieu of sandbags for erosion and seepage control purposes, particularly at the crest of levees to increase the functional height of the levee. Hesco baskets can also be used to create walls to protect personnel as a force protection barrier system (MIL-DTL-32488 2014).
key_points: Gabions are galvanized or PVC-coated wire containers filled with 4–8 inch stone; PVC coating required when pH >12 or <6, or high organic acid concentration.
Designed as mass gravity structures using the same procedures as rigid retaining walls (Figure 4-27).
Vertical-face gabion walls should be battered ~6° to keep the resultant force toward the back of the wall.
Base interface friction angle equals effective stress friction angle of the foundation; δ/φ′ = 0.9 at the back of the wall.
Geosynthetic or granular filter required when backfill is predominantly sand to prevent erosion into gabions.
Gabion counterforts (headers) recommended for clay slopes, spaced 13 ft (very soft clay) to 30 ft (stiff clay), extending at least one gabion length beyond the critical slip circle.
Hesco baskets (geotextile-lined wire cages) are a related system used for erosion control, levee height increase, and force protection barriers (MIL-DTL-32488 2014).

sections.applicability: Applies when designing gabion retaining walls or Hesco bastion systems for erosion control, slope stabilization, earth retention, or force protection.

sections.title: Earth-Filled Crib Walls and Bin Walls
sections.summary: Describes crib walls and bin walls as mass gravity retaining structures suitable where site access limits use of other wall types. They are designed using the same methodology as rigid retaining walls (Figure 4-27), illustrated in Figure 4-33, with a general height limit of 30 feet; taller walls should use more robust alternatives.
sections.body: Crib walls and bin walls can be used as retaining structures when site access is too difficult to use other earth retaining structures. These also are designed as mass gravity structures using the same design methodology presented in Figure 4-27. Examples of the design elements of crib and bin walls are shown in Figure 4-33. The height of crib and bin walls should generally be less than 30 feet. For taller walls, consideration should be given to other wall types that are generally more robust.
key_points: Crib and bin walls are appropriate when site access is too difficult for other retaining structure types.
Designed as mass gravity structures using the same methodology as rigid retaining walls (Figure 4-27).
Wall height should generally not exceed 30 feet; taller walls warrant consideration of more robust wall types.
Design elements illustrated in Figure 4-33.
figures: Figure 4-33 Design Elements of Crib Walls and Bin Walls
sections.applicability: Applies when designing earth-filled crib or bin walls, particularly in sites with difficult access, for walls generally not exceeding 30 feet in height.

sections.title: Anchored Bulkhead Design — Example Scenarios Summary
sections.summary: Summarizes key design details illustrated across the free-earth method example scenarios for anchored sheet pile bulkheads, covering interface friction assumptions, factor of safety application to passive pressure, penetration depth increases for scour, and bending moment reduction using Rowe's diagram. Covers Scenarios 1–3 including socketed/toed pile cases.
sections.body:
Important design details illustrated in the example scenarios are as follows:
1) The effects of interface friction between the wall and soil are only considered for passive pressure in granular soils. Wall friction is ignored in all other cases.
2) A factor of safety is applied to the passive pressure determination below the dredge line, and for passive pressures calculated for the anchor.
3) The calculated depth of penetration below the dredge line (D) is increased by 20% to allow for scour, additional dredging, etc.
4) The calculated bending moment in the sheet pile is reduced using Figure 4-36.

Scenario 1 is the general case for the free-earth method. The step-by-step method, indicated on Figure 4-37 would be appropriate for coarse-grained soils, with the material below the dredge line being similar to the soil retained by the wall. The soil properties used for the layers would be drained or effective stress parameters (c′ and φ′). For the calculation of the earth pressures, moist or total unit weights are used above the landside water table elevation, and effective or buoyant unit weights are used below the water table. The net water pressure applied to the landside of the wall decreases from the dredge line elevation to a value of zero at depth, D, to account for seepage effects.

Scenario 2 is similar, but a different method is needed to determine the design moment in the sheet pile. For this example, the sheet pile is driven into a dense granular soil. If the wall system is less flexible as reflected by the value of ρ (Figure 4-36), the moment is calculated assuming that the wall behaves like a simply-supported beam.

Scenario 3 in Figure 4-37 shows a case where the sheet pile is socketed or toed into a very hard material (rock or hardpan). Since no displacement occurs at the tip of the sheet pile, the passive pressure decreases to zero at the surface of the hard foundation. The moment is not reduced using Rowe's diagram (Figure 4-36).
key_points: Interface friction between wall and soil is only considered for passive pressure in granular soils; ignored in all other cases.
A factor of safety is applied to passive pressure below the dredge line and for anchor passive pressures.
Calculated penetration depth D is increased by 20% to account for scour and additional dredging.
Bending moment in sheet pile is reduced using Rowe's diagram (Figure 4-36), except for socketed/toed piles (Scenario 3).
Scenario 1 (free-earth method): uses drained/effective stress parameters; buoyant unit weights below water table; seepage accounted for by net water pressure tapering to zero at depth D.
Scenario 2: moment calculated assuming simply-supported beam behavior when wall system is less flexible (based on ρ value).
Scenario 3: pile toed into rock/hardpan — passive pressure decreases to zero at hard foundation surface; Rowe's moment reduction not applied.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing anchored sheet pile bulkheads using the free-earth method across varied soil and embedment conditions (granular soils, dense granular, and rock/hardpan toe scenarios).

sections.title: Factored Passive Resistance
sections.summary: Describes the two methods used to incorporate an adequate factor of safety for passive resistance in the stability analysis of flexible retaining structures. Where passive earth pressure forces are directly calculated, defines the allowable passive force (PP,allow) as the governing design quantity. Applies to base-of-wall and anchor passive resistance evaluation.
sections.body: As noted above, the stability of many flexible structures depends on the passive resistance at the base of the wall and in front of supporting anchors. key_points: Stability of flexible structures is often governed by passive resistance at the wall base and in front of anchors.
Two distinct methods are available to apply an adequate factor of safety to passive resistance.
When passive earth pressure forces are computed directly, the design quantity is the allowable passive force (PP,allow).

sections.title: Anchored Bulkheads
sections.summary: Covers the design of anchored bulkhead waterfront structures including sheet pile types, failure modes, earth and water pressure distributions, free vs. fixed earth support analysis methods, and Rowe's moment reduction for flexible walls. Provides equations for relative wall flexibility and design scenarios with multiple soil layers, surcharges, and differential water levels.
sections.body:
Anchored bulkheads are waterfront structures used to allow a change in elevation for access to the water. These structures are often driven sheet piles that are restrained on the landside by some form of anchoring system. Sheet piles are often steel, but can also be made of concrete, wood, vinyl, and plastic. Excavations are made on the waterside down to the dredge line to allow sufficient draft for vessels. The dredge line is the lowest depth to which soil is removed in front of the wall.

Several references are available that provide design guidance and construction details for anchored bulkheads. These include:
• USACE (1995b) Design of Coastal Revetments, Seawalls, and Bulkheads, EM 1110-2-1614, CECW-EH-D.
• USACE (1994a) Design of Sheet Pile Walls, CECW-ED, EM 1110-2-2504.
• US Steel (1984) Steel Sheet Piling Design Manual, Updated and reprinted by the US Department of Transportation/FHWA.

The earth pressure and water pressure distributions on anchored bulkheads can be quite complex. The ground surface elevation is different on the landside and the waterside. The water level on the landside and waterside is often different as well. In addition to soil and water loads, the anchoring system applies a concentrated force on the wall. Anchored bulkheads are often constructed by excavation and dredging in natural soils or unengineered fills; therefore, the soil properties can vary greatly. An important part of the engineering design of these structures is to accurately simplify the cross section and soil parameters into relatively homogeneous layers that can be accommodated by earth pressure theory.

Anchored bulkheads can be designed by determining the appropriate pressures acting on each side of the wall separately. Sometimes, it is more convenient to use net pressure diagrams, where the difference in the pressure on each side of the wall is calculated. Examples of a total pressure diagram and a net pressure diagram are shown in Figure 4-34.

Anchored bulkheads can be designed using limit equilibrium methods. An important element in using limit equilibrium methods is to define the possible modes of failure. Anchored bulkheads can fail in many different ways, as shown in Figure 4-35. A proper design will examine each potential mode of failure of the different anchored bulkhead elements. Interlock failure should also be considered.

Methods for the analysis of anchored bulkheads are often categorized into free earth or fixed earth support methods. The difference between these two methods involves the behavior of the wall below the dredge line. In free earth analysis, the passive resistance below the dredge line is not developed to the point that movement of the sheet pile tip is prevented. The tip of the sheet pile can deflect toward the water side. The free earth support system tends to overpredict the bending moments in the sheet pile, and techniques are available to correct the bending moment. In fixed earth analysis, which is less commonly used, the lower end of the wall is essentially fixed so that no movement is allowed.

Experience and scale model testing have shown that the free earth support method overpredicts the bending moment in flexible walls (Rowe 1952). The differences from theory are explained by flexural of the wall but above and below the dredge line. Corrections to the predicted moment, often referred to as moment reduction, depend on the relative flexibility (ρ) of the wall, which is defined as Eq. 4-31.

The relative flexibility is used with Figure 4-36 to determine the ratio of the design moment to the theoretical moment. The moment is reduced for walls that penetrate into medium dense or better sand. The moment is not reduced for penetration into fine-grained soils or loose sands.

Three example scenarios showing the design steps for anchored bulkheads are shown in Figure 4-37. These examples are complex in that they have the following characteristics:
1) Two or more layers of soil,
2) Backfill loaded by point load (Q) and surcharge area (q), and
3) Different interior and exterior water levels. The difference in the water pressures is accommodated by a trapezoidal unbalanced water pressure distribution.
key_points: Anchored bulkheads are sheet pile structures restrained by a landside anchor; sheet piles may be steel, concrete, wood, vinyl, or plastic (vinyl/plastic not suitable where failure consequences are severe).
Design must account for differing ground surface elevations, differential water levels (trapezoidal unbalanced water pressure), and concentrated anchor forces.
Pressure can be evaluated as total pressures on each side separately or as a net pressure diagram (Figure 4-34).
All failure modes must be checked: Figure 4-35 shows the full range; interlock failure must also be considered.
Free earth support (tip can deflect waterside) overpredicts bending moments in flexible walls; Rowe's moment reduction (Figure 4-36) corrects this for penetration into medium-dense or better sands.
Relative wall flexibility ρ = (H + D)⁴ / EI governs moment reduction per Eq. 4-31; no reduction applied for penetration into fine-grained soils or loose sands.
Fixed earth support (tip fixed, no movement) is less commonly used.

equations.description: Relative flexibility of anchored sheet pile wall: ρ = (H + D)⁴ / EI, where H = exposed height (in), D = depth of penetration below dredge line (in), E = Young's modulus (psi), I = moment of inertia (in⁴/ft). Used with Figure 4-36 for Rowe's moment reduction.

sections.title: Anchor Design
sections.summary: Covers the design of anchor systems for anchored bulkheads, focusing on deadman anchors. Addresses anchor types, depth of construction, location relative to the active failure wedge, calculation of continuous wall anchor capacity (including interface friction and reduced capacity near active wedge), and differences between wall anchors and individual anchor blocks. References FHWA GEC No. 4 for additional anchor types.
sections.body:
Various types of anchors can be used with anchored bulkheads. Examples of different anchor systems are given in Figure 4-38. The deadman anchor has been historically popular and its design incorporates earth pressure theory. Deadman anchors can be discrete individual elements, or they can be a continuous reinforced concrete wall parallel to the bulkhead. Anchors are normally constructed to a depth equal to twice the anchor height. The distance between the anchor and the wall is important. In order to maximize the capacity, the anchor needs to be located outside of the potential failure wedge. Figure 4-39(a) provides guidance on the location of a deadman anchor relative to the active wedge.

The equations for calculating the capacity of a continuous wall anchor are shown in Figure 4-39(b). The interface friction angle between the anchor and soil is considered in the determination of the passive earth pressure coefficient. The calculated passive resistance of the anchor is dependent on where the anchor is located. A reduced anchor capacity results for anchors placed close to the active failure wedge. Figure 4-40 shows a section view of the wall anchor in Figure 4-39. The differences in the capacity of wall anchors versus individual anchor blocks are summarized.

The FHWA Geotechnical Engineering Circular No. 4 - Ground Anchors and Anchored Systems (FHWA 1999) provides design procedures for many different types of anchors.
key_points: Deadman anchors can be discrete elements or a continuous reinforced concrete wall parallel to the bulkhead.
Anchors are normally constructed to a depth equal to twice the anchor height.
Anchor must be located outside the potential active failure wedge to maximize capacity; Figure 4-39(a) provides location guidance.
Continuous wall anchor capacity equations (Figure 4-39(b)) account for interface friction angle in passive earth pressure coefficient determination.
Anchor capacity is reduced when the anchor is placed close to the active failure wedge.
Wall anchor capacity differs from individual anchor block capacity; differences are summarized in Figure 4-40.
FHWA Geotechnical Engineering Circular No. 4 (FHWA 1999) provides design procedures for many anchor types.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting, locating, and sizing anchor systems (particularly deadman anchors) for anchored bulkhead wall design.

sections.title: Cantilever Flexible Walls
sections.summary: Covers design of cantilever flexible walls (typically sheet piling) that support soil without anchors or bracing. Describes net pressure diagrams, step-by-step penetration depth (D) determination for effective stress conditions, and two design charts for simple stratigraphy: one for sand and one for sand overlying saturated clay. Addresses factoring of KP and increasing D for scour/dredging.
sections.body:
A cantilever flexible wall supports the soil without anchors or bracing. These walls are commonly constructed from sheet piling and can be used as earth retention structures for exposed wall heights less than about 15 feet. Stiffer types of flexible structure may be able to support higher walls. The pattern of deflection of the sheet pile results in complex earth pressures acting on the wall. Figure 4-41 shows the net pressure diagram for cantilever sheet piling. The designer should be aware of cases where there is a difference in the water level on each side of the wall. The figure shows a step-by-step approach to determine the depth of penetration (D) for design of a cantilever flexible wall for effective stress conditions.

Two charts are available to simplify the cantilever wall calculations for sites with simple stratigraphy. Figure 4-42 allows the penetration depth (D) to be determined for a site consisting of coarse-grained soil that can be characterized by a single value of effective stress friction angle. A phreatic surface can be accommodated assuming that the level is the same on both sides of the sheet pile. There are two families of curves on the chart, with one used for determining the maximum moment in the sheet pile and the other for determining the embedment depth. This chart was developed assuming that the total unit weight of the soil was 124.8 pcf, which is twice the buoyant unit weight. An example of the use of this chart for a cantilever sheet pile wall with a height of 15 ft in a coarse-grained soil is given in Figure 4-43.

The value of KP used with Figure 4-42 should be factored as described in Section 4-7.1. In addition, the final value of D should be increased by about 20% to design against future dredging or scour.

The second chart (Figure 4-44) was developed for a sand layer overlying a saturated clay layer. The sand layer extends down to the dredge line. The sand layer is characterized by φ′, and the clay layer is assigned a single undrained strength (su). The effective stress at dredge level in the sand layer should be calculated based on the position of the water table using the appropriate unit weights. An example using this chart is shown in Figure 4-45.

A wall designed using Figure 4-44 is supported by passive pressure associated with the undrained shear strength of the clay. The undrained shear strength can be factored as indicated in the figure. The strength is factored only on the passive side of the wall, which leads to the equation provided. This approach allows an explicit consideration of F. Alternatively, if the full undrained shear strength is used, the penetration depth must be increased by 30% to 40% to allow for a factor of safety. The magnitude of F is unknown with the latter approach.

The US Steel (USS) Sheet Piling Design Manual (USS 1984) contains more details about the design of cantilever sheet piles in coarse-grained and fine-grained soils and provides additional design examples.
key_points: Cantilever flexible walls (typically sheet piling) are suitable for exposed wall heights less than ~15 ft; stiffer structures may support greater heights.
Net pressure distribution on cantilever sheet piling is complex due to the deflection pattern; designers must account for differential water levels on each side.
Figure 4-41 provides a step-by-step procedure to determine penetration depth D under effective stress conditions.
Figure 4-42 (sand) and Figure 4-44 (sand over clay) are design charts that simplify penetration depth and maximum moment calculations for simple stratigraphy.
KP used with Figure 4-42 must be factored per Section 4-7.1; the computed D should then be increased by ~20% to account for future dredging or scour.

For sand-over-clay conditions (Figure 4-44), undrained shear strength su is factored on the passive side to achieve an explicit factor of safety F; alternatively, D must be increased 30–40% if full su is used.
Chart in Figure 4-42 assumes total unit weight of 124.8 pcf (twice the buoyant unit weight); verify applicability to site conditions.

sections.title: Soldier Pile Walls
sections.summary: Describes the components and construction sequence of soldier pile and lagging walls, where discrete vertical soldier piles support horizontal lagging to transfer earth pressures. Covers pile installation in drilled shafts, concrete securement below dredge line, top-down lagging placement during excavation, and support options including cantilever design for strong soil or rock conditions.
sections.body: Soldier pile and lagging walls consist of discrete vertical soldier piles (or beams) that support horizontal lagging as shown in Figure 4-46. The lagging transfers earth pressures from the soil to the soldier piles. In the typical construction sequence, the soldier piles are placed in shafts drilled prior to excavation for the wall. Concrete is used to secure the soldier pile in place below the dredge line. Above the dredge line, the shafts are often backfilled with low strength concrete or flowable fill. As excavation proceeds adjacent to the soldier piles, lagging is placed between the piles from the top down. Soldier pile and lagging walls may be supported internally or externally. A cantilever design can be used if strong soil or rock is present at the base of the wall and the soldier piles are sufficiently stiff.
key_points: Soldier pile and lagging walls use discrete vertical piles (beams) with horizontal lagging spanning between them to retain soil.
Lagging transfers earth pressures from soil to the soldier piles; it does not act as a continuous wall element.
Soldier piles are installed in pre-drilled shafts before excavation begins; concrete secures piles below the dredge line.
Above the dredge line, shafts are typically backfilled with low-strength concrete or flowable fill.
Lagging is installed top-down as excavation progresses alongside the piles.
Walls may be internally or externally supported; cantilever design is viable where strong soil or rock exists at the wall base and piles are sufficiently stiff.
figures: Figure 4-46 Soldier Pile and Lagging Walls – (a) Section View, (b) Elevation and Plan View, (c) Passive Pressure Assumptions, and (d) Example Calculation
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or evaluating soldier pile and lagging walls for earth retention in excavation support systems.

sections.title: Secant Pile Walls and Tangent Pile Walls
sections.summary: Covers secant and tangent pile walls as alternatives to sheet pile and soldier pile walls where greater lateral stiffness is needed. Describes construction methods, seepage resistance characteristics, reinforcement approaches, and notes that deformation-based analysis procedures are typically used for design, especially for tied-back configurations in deep or deformation-sensitive excavations.
sections.body:
Secant and tangent pile walls are alternatives to sheet pile walls and soldier pile walls where greater lateral stiffness is required. As discussed in Section 2-4, the increased stiffness reduces vertical deformations at the ground surface adjacent to the wall. Neither secant nor tangent pile walls require the time-consuming lagging installation required for soldier pile walls.

Secant pile walls are constructed by installing primary and secondary concrete shafts that overlap (Figure 4-47). First, the primary shafts are drilled, with the position of the shafts aligned by a template and the template controlling the distance between primary shafts. The concrete shafts are constructed without reinforcement. The secondary shafts are drilled between the primary piles such that they intersect the piles on both sides of the alignment. The secondary piles are reinforced with steel rebar cages or with steel beams (W sections). Secant pile walls have an additional benefit over sheet pile walls and soldier pile walls in that well-constructed secant pile walls provide a seepage barrier.

Tangent pile walls are constructed such that there is no overlap between piles (Figure 4-48). Ideally, the shafts are drilled such that they are tangent to the adjacent piles, but there is often a space between shafts. The shafts are reinforced with steel beams (I or W sections) or rebar cages. Tangent pile walls do not have the same seepage resistance as secant pile walls, since gaps are often present between piles. Also, clean sands may ravel or run between the piles in tangent pile walls.

Secant and tangent pile walls are often tied-back, especially when deformations outside of the excavation must be controlled or if the excavations are deep. Since controlling deformations is a key factor in the selection of secant and tangent pile walls, analysis procedures often are based on calculating deformations as opposed to determining factor of safety.
key_points: Secant and tangent pile walls offer greater lateral stiffness than sheet pile or soldier pile walls, reducing ground surface settlements adjacent to excavations.
Secant pile walls use overlapping primary (unreinforced) and secondary (reinforced) concrete shafts, providing a seepage barrier when well-constructed.
Tangent pile walls have no overlap between shafts; gaps are often present, reducing seepage resistance and allowing clean sands to ravel or run between piles.
Both wall types eliminate the need for time-consuming lagging installation required by soldier pile walls.
Secondary piles in secant walls are reinforced with steel rebar cages or W-section steel beams; tangent pile shafts use I/W sections or rebar cages.
Secant and tangent pile walls are frequently tied-back for deep excavations or where deformation control is critical.
Design analysis for these wall types is typically deformation-based rather than factor-of-safety-based.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and designing secant or tangent pile walls as retention systems for excavations requiring high lateral stiffness and/or deformation control.

sections.title: Soil Nail Walls
sections.summary: Covers soil nail wall design, construction, and applicability. Describes soil nailing as a top-down method for permanent excavation support using passive steel reinforcing bars or tendons in grout-filled holes. Addresses suitable and adverse soil conditions, nail geometry, spacing, drainage, facing installation, and references FHWA GEC No. 7 for detailed design and inspection procedures.
sections.body:
Soil nailing is a method to create a reinforced soil mass for the purpose of long-term support of permanent excavations. Detailed design, construction, and inspection procedures for soil nail walls can be found in Geotechnical Engineering Circular No. 7 (FHWA 2015).

Soil nail walls can be a cost-effective wall system for sites with limited right-of-way or overhead restrictions. The equipment used for constructing these types of walls is commonly available and limited in size, so these walls can be constructed at remote sites. This type of wall system also accommodates curves in the wall alignment better than other wall types.

A soil nail is commonly a steel reinforcing bar or steel tendon placed in a grout-filled hole. The reinforcing element acts passively, in that it is not post-tensioned. A soil-nail wall is constructed using a top down method where soil nails and shotcrete are installed as the excavation progresses. The nails are placed on a vertical spacing of 3 to 5 feet and a horizontal spacing of 4 to 6 feet. The soil nails are often oriented at 15 degrees below horizontal. Strip drains are typically installed at regular spacing between the nails to prevent water from collecting behind the facing. After the full depth of excavation is achieved, a final shotcrete or concrete facing is installed. A cross section of a soil nail wall is shown in Figure 4-49. The length of the soil nails is often around 70% of the height of the wall, but specific design cases may require longer or shorter nails.

Soil nail walls are best suited for soil deposits which can sustain vertical cuts of 4 to 6 feet for up to 48 hours to allow for the installation of the nails. In addition, it is desired that the drill holes remain open during the tendon installation and grouting. Soil deposits that have proven appropriate for soil nail wall construction include dense granular soils, weathered rock, stiff fine-grained soils, stiff residual soils, and some glacial tills. Adverse soil conditions include dry, uniform, granular soils, pervious soils with high phreatic surfaces, soils with cobbles and boulders, and soft organic and inorganic fine-grained soil.

Soil nail walls are designed for long-term support; therefore, drained shear strength parameters are normally required for design. For walls constructed to support stiff, overconsolidated soils, fully softened strengths obtained from triaxial or direct shear testing are used. For walls constructed in weaker saturated fine-grained soils, it may be prudent to determine undrained strengths to assess if the unsupported slope is stable during excavation for the depth of the excavation stage. Undrained strengths might also be necessary for basal heave calculations (Section 2-4.3.3).
key_points: Soil nail walls use passive (non-post-tensioned) steel bars or tendons grouted into drilled holes; constructed top-down as excavation progresses.
Typical nail spacing: 3–5 ft vertical, 4–6 ft horizontal; nails typically oriented 15° below horizontal; nail length is often ~70% of wall height.
Strip drains are installed between nails to prevent water buildup behind the facing; final shotcrete or cast-in-place concrete facing is applied after full excavation.

Best suited for soils that can sustain 4–6 ft vertical cuts for up to 48 hours; suitable soils include dense granular, weathered rock, stiff fine-grained, stiff residual soils, and some glacial tills.
Adverse conditions include dry uniform granular soils, pervious soils with high phreatic surfaces, cobbles/boulders, and soft organic or inorganic fine-grained soils.
Drained shear strength parameters are normally required for design; undrained strengths may be needed for excavation stability or basal heave checks in weaker saturated fine-grained soils.
Detailed design, construction, and inspection procedures are provided in FHWA Geotechnical Engineering Circular No. 7 (FHWA 2015).
