sections.title: EXCAVATION SUPPORT
sections.summary: Introduces excavation support as a critical element of excavation design, explaining that flexible retaining structures often require internal or external support systems. Covers the complexity of forces acting on support elements due to wall-soil-support interaction, and notes that earth pressure distributions are based on case history measurements from instrumented excavations.
sections.body: Flexible retaining structures are an important part of excavation design, which has been discussed in detail in Chapter 2. In many cases, the retaining walls for excavations must be supported, either internally or externally. Determining the forces that act on the support system elements is an important part of the excavation design. The interaction between the wall, soil, and support system makes the forces quite complex. The forces depend on the rate of construction, the distance between supports, the installation quality, etc. The earth pressure distributions were based largely on case history measurements from instrumented excavations and are presented in the following section. These pressure distributions are then used to determine the forces that must be resisted by internal or external support.
key_points: Excavation support systems may be internal (cross-lot braces, rakers) or external (ground anchors/tiebacks).
Forces on support elements are complex, depending on construction rate, support spacing, and installation quality.
Earth pressure distributions used in design are based largely on case history measurements from instrumented excavations.
Apparent earth pressure diagrams are used to determine forces resisted by internal or external support.
sections.applicability: Applies to all excavation designs requiring internal or external support of flexible retaining structures.

sections.title: Apparent Earth Pressure Diagrams
sections.summary: Describes the semi-empirical basis for apparent earth pressure diagrams used in supported flexible retaining structure design. Explains that diagrams were developed from measured support loads on real projects, peak pressures are tied to the active earth pressure coefficient KA, and separate diagram sets exist for internally braced vs. externally supported (FHWA 1999) systems. Covers two methods—tributary area and hinge—for calculating strut forces.
sections.body:
Earth pressures for supported flexible retaining structures have been semi-empirically determined based on measured support loads on engineering projects. The pressure diagrams were drawn to encompass the measured earth pressures, and actual pressures are likely lower than those shown. They are referred to as apparent earth pressure diagrams because of this semi-empirical basis. However, the diagrams have a basis in earth pressure theory in that the peak pressures are calculated with values of the active earth pressure coefficient, KA. The shape of the diagrams depends on the vertical location of support force application (struts or anchors). Apparent pressure diagrams are used for the design of internally- and externally-supported excavations.

The apparent earth pressure diagrams are provided in Figure 4-51 through Figure 4-53. The magnitude and shape of the diagrams depend on the soil type. One set of apparent earth pressure diagrams has been historically used for internally braced support systems (Terzaghi and Peck 1967). A different set of pressure diagrams was developed for externally supported systems (FHWA 1999). These diagrams were developed because of differences in when the supports are installed, the amount of displacement that can occur prior to support installation, and the magnitude of the preload applied to the support elements. It is up to the judgement of the design engineer to decide if the FHWA (1999) apparent earth pressure diagrams should be used for both internally- and externally-braced support structures, particularly when the struts are preloaded for excavation bracing.

The horizontal strut force, represented as T on the apparent earth pressure diagrams, is determined by using the earth pressure distribution in one of two different ways: (1) tributary area and (2) hinge method. For the tributary area method, the load on each strut is calculated using the assumption that a strut carries the pressures existing from one-half the vertical distance to the strut above to one-half the vertical distance to the strut below. The hinge method is based on summing moments about strut locations (e.g., 'hinges' where moment = 0) to calculate specific strut loads.

In general, the apparent pressure diagrams were developed for fairly deep (> 20 ft) excavations that are relatively wide.
key_points: Apparent earth pressure diagrams are semi-empirical, drawn to encompass measured support loads; actual pressures are typically lower.
Peak pressures are calculated using the active earth pressure coefficient KA; diagram shape depends on vertical support location.
Separate diagram sets exist for internally braced systems (Terzaghi & Peck 1967) and externally supported systems (FHWA 1999).
Strut forces (T) are calculated by either the tributary area method or the hinge method.
Diagrams were developed for deep (> 20 ft), relatively wide excavations; engineering judgment is needed for other conditions.
Engineer must judge whether FHWA 1999 diagrams should be used for both internally and externally braced systems when struts are preloaded.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and applying apparent earth pressure diagrams for design of internally or externally supported flexible retaining structures in excavations.

sections.title: Stability of Base of Excavations
sections.summary: Highlights the importance of basal stability in excavation design, noting it is a potential failure mechanism and can also influence the earth pressure on the wall. Refers the reader to Section 2-4.3 for detailed procedures on evaluating basal stability of excavations.
sections.body: The stability of the base of excavations is very important in that it is a potential failure mechanism for cuts. In addition, the base stability can also influence the earth pressure applied to the wall. Section 2-4.3 provides information regarding the basal stability of excavations.
key_points: Basal stability is a critical potential failure mechanism for excavations.
Base stability conditions also influence the earth pressure applied to the retaining wall.
Detailed procedures for basal stability assessment are provided in Section 2-4.3.
sections.applicability: Applies to any excavation design where base heave or basal failure is a potential concern.

sections.title: Internal Support (Excavation Bracing)
sections.summary: Covers internal support systems for excavations, including cross-lot braces and rakers. Notes that once support loads are predicted using apparent earth pressure diagrams, the design of the internal support elements is primarily a structural engineering task. Introduces subsections for narrow excavations and raking braces.
sections.body: Internal support or excavation bracing refers to support systems that are inside of the excavation, such as cross-lot braces or rakers (Figure 2-6). Once the support loads are predicted, the design of internal support is primarily a structural engineering task.
key_points: Internal support systems include cross-lot braces and rakers located inside the excavation.
After support loads are determined from apparent earth pressure diagrams, design of the bracing is primarily a structural task.
Subsections address special procedures for narrow braced excavations and excavations with raking braces.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing internally braced excavation support systems using cross-lot braces or rakers.

sections.title: Internally-Braced Narrow Excavations
sections.summary: Presents special design procedures for narrow braced excavations supported by flexible walls. Describes a five-step design process covering base stability, strut force calculation, wall and wale section design with arching reduction (80% of full pressure for all but upper span), recomputation using active earth pressures at each construction stage, and selection of the controlling design case.
sections.body:
Special design procedures are applied for narrow braced excavations. The design steps for a narrow cut supported by a flexible wall are shown in Figure 4-54. The appropriate apparent earth pressure diagrams are used to determine the pressure distribution above the excavation depth. The unbalanced water pressures need to be considered if the retained water table is above the base of the excavation. An example for this type of design is presented in Figure 4-55.

The basic procedure for the design of walls for narrow cuts is as follows:
1) Calculate the factor of safety for base stability using the procedures shown in Section 2-4.3.
2) Compute the strut forces as outlined in Figure 4-54.
3) Compute the required section for the wall and wale. In computing the required wall section, arching could be accounted for by reducing the pressures in all but the upper span. A reduction of 80% of the values shown is appropriate.
4) Recompute the strut forces and the required sections of the wall and wales using active earth pressures at each stage instead of the active earth pressure diagrams (similar to Figure 4-56).
5) Compare the strut forces and required sections computed in Step 4 to Step 3, and select the larger force or section for design.
key_points: Narrow braced excavations require special design procedures separate from general apparent earth pressure diagram application.
Unbalanced water pressure must be included when the retained water table is above the excavation base.
Arching effect allows an 80% pressure reduction for all spans except the uppermost span when computing required wall section.
Design must also consider active earth pressures at each construction stage (staged analysis using Figure 4-56 approach).
Final design uses the larger of the forces/sections from the apparent pressure diagram approach vs. the staged active pressure approach.
sections.applicability: Applies specifically to design of internally braced, narrow excavations supported by flexible walls.

sections.title: Internally-Braced Excavations with Raking Braces
sections.summary: Addresses design of flexible walls supported by raking braces (rakers), where significant wall displacement may occur before support installation. Indicates that in this condition an active earth pressure distribution governs. Notes that this arrangement is typically for temporary support, and that unbalanced water load must be considered. References Figure 4-56 for the earth pressure distribution and design steps.
sections.body: When a wall is supported by raking braces, considerable displacement of the wall may occur prior to the installation of support elements. Figure 4-56 shows the earth pressure distribution on a flexible wall where wall displacements created an active earth pressure condition. This arrangement would be for temporary support. The unbalanced water load needs to be considered in this cross section.
key_points: Raking brace (raker) support systems allow significant wall displacement before installation, mobilizing active earth pressure conditions.
Active earth pressure distribution (not apparent pressure diagrams) governs design for walls with raking braces.
This support arrangement is typically used for temporary conditions only.
Unbalanced water load must be included in the design cross section.
Design steps are illustrated in Figure 4-56.
sections.applicability: Applies to design of flexible retaining walls supported by raking braces (rakers) in temporary excavation support situations.

sections.title: External Support (Tied Back Walls)
sections.summary: Covers tied back wall design using ground anchors as external support, which keeps the excavation interior clear. Explains differences from internally braced systems including earlier anchor installation and preloading that limits displacement. References FHWA (1999) GEC No. 4 for detailed procedures and lists the first four of the FHWA design steps, covering project requirements, site investigation, design properties/factors of safety, and lateral earth pressure distribution selection.
sections.body:
Tied back walls use external support, such as ground anchors, to provide stability and offer distinct advantages compared to internally-braced support systems. For excavation bracing, tied back walls keep the excavation open since the support elements are located outside of the excavation footprint. Tied back walls can be either temporary or permanent structures. The wall elements can be sheet piles, soldier beams and lagging, diaphragm walls, or other wall systems.

The FHWA Geotechnical Engineering Circular No. 4 (FHWA 1999) provides design details that can be applied to internally braced excavations. Many of the basic procedures shown for excavation bracing and anchored bulkheads are used for tied back walls. However, the anchors (tie-backs) can be installed earlier in wall construction. The anchors are preloaded and prevent significant displacement from occurring. For this reason, tied back wall design uses apparent earth pressure diagrams that are different than those used for internally supported excavation bracing. The apparent earth pressure diagrams for externally supported retaining structures are shown on the right side of Figure 4-51 through Figure 4-53.

For sands and stiff clays, the position of the top and bottom support must be known. The reaction force, R, is based on the passive resistance of the soil, and a factor of safety of 1.5 should be applied to this resistance. The depth of penetration, D, is selected to obtain the correct value of the passive resistance. A δ/φʹ ratio equal to 0.5 to 1.0 can be used in the passive resistance calculation. Table 4-1 should be consulted for the value of δ. KP should be obtained from Figure 4-12.

The design of tied back walls is complex, and a proper design consists of numerous steps. Compared to internally-braced excavations, externally-braced excavations have many additional elements that are geotechnical (as opposed to structural) in nature. FHWA (1999) outlines the individual steps, and these are given below:
1) Establish project requirements, including all geometry, external loading conditions (temporary and/or permanent, seismic, etc.), performance criteria, and construction constraints.
2) Evaluate site subsurface conditions and relevant properties of in situ soil and rock.
3) Evaluate design properties, establish design factors of safety or load and resistance factors, and select level of corrosion protection.
4) Select lateral earth pressure distribution acting on the back of the wall for final wall height. Add appropriate water, surcharge, and seismic pressures.
key_points: Tied back walls use ground anchors external to the excavation, keeping the work area clear of internal bracing.
Anchors are preloaded and installed earlier than internal braces, limiting wall displacement and requiring different apparent earth pressure diagrams.
Apparent earth pressure diagrams for externally supported structures (FHWA 1999) are shown on the right side of Figures 4-51 through 4-53.
For sands and stiff clays, a factor of safety of 1.5 must be applied to passive resistance used for wall penetration depth design.
δ/φʹ ratio of 0.5 to 1.0 is used for passive resistance calculation; Table 4-1 and Figure 4-12 provide δ and KP values respectively.
FHWA (1999) GEC No. 4 is the primary reference for tied back wall design steps.
Tied back wall design includes significant geotechnical elements beyond the structural design required for internally braced systems.
sections.applicability: Applies to design of tied back (externally supported) retaining walls for temporary or permanent excavation support using ground anchors.

sections.title: CELLULAR COFFERDAM DESIGN
sections.summary: Covers the design principles, geometry configurations, loading cases, and failure modes for cellular sheet pile cofferdams. Explains how cofferdams are transformed into equivalent parallel wall sections for hand calculations, discusses phreatic surface assumptions, and enumerates all loading conditions and failure modes that must be assessed, referencing Table 4-7 and key references (USS 1984; USACE 1989).
sections.body:
Cellular sheet pile cofferdams are structures constructed from sheet piles driven in a variety of geometries and filled with soil. Cofferdams perform many purposes, such as creating dewatered construction areas, lock walls, retaining structures, mooring structures, and spillway weirs.

Cofferdam geometries include circular cells, semicircular cells, and cloverleaf cells. These different configurations are shown in Figure 4-57(a). For hand calculations, these configurations are transformed into equivalent parallel wall cofferdams of width, B. The strict definition of B is that it is the width of a rectangular section that has a sectional modulus equivalent to that of the actual cofferdam cell. Since this can be a difficult calculation, approximate methods to calculate B for the different cofferdam cell configurations are shown on Figure 4-57(a).

Figure 4-57(b) shows a typical section used for cofferdam design. In some designs, there may be soil against the outboard face, and the berm may not be present on the inboard face.

Many factors must be considered in the design of cellular cofferdams. Because of the complexity involved in cofferdam design, numerical methods modeling soil-structure interaction are often used. The stability of cofferdams depends on ratio of the width to the height, the resistance of an inboard berm, if any, and the type and permeability of cell fill materials. Usually active and/or passive pressures act on exterior faces of the sheeting. The shear strength of the cofferdam fill material is a very important factor in the overall stability of cofferdams. Equally important is the line of saturation or phreatic surface in the cell fill. The position of the water surface or line of saturation in the cell fill is usually determined by the soil type used. For coarse-grained, free-draining fill, a slope of 1H:1V is assumed. For fine-grained, poorly-draining cell fill, a slope of 3H:1V is often used. In some cases, the line of saturation is assumed to extend from the outboard face of the cofferdam to the top elevation of the berm on the outside of the inboard face. The inboard ground surface or berm also may have an elevated phreatic surface, but the stabilizing effect of the inboard face water pressure is often ignored in design calculations (USS 1984; USACE 1989).

Many different loading cases and failure conditions are used to assess the stability and performance of cofferdams. The main loading conditions are: Case I – maximum pool conditions, Case II – initial filling conditions, and Case III – drawdown conditions (USACE 1989). For each of these loading conditions, the following modes of failure must be assessed:
• Sliding
• Overturning
• Rotation (Hansen method)
• Deep seated sliding
• Bearing capacity
• Settlement
• Seepage
• Interlock tension
• Vertical shear resistance (Terzaghi method)
• Horizontal shear resistance (Cummings method)
• Vertical shear resistance (Schroeder-Maitland method)
• Pullout of outboard sheets
• Penetration of inboard sheets

Some of the analysis methods, such as overturning, are very similar to those used for gravity retaining walls (Section 4-5.1). Other modes of failure are unique to cellular cofferdams and were developed specifically for the various modes of failure. Many of the failure modes employ earth pressure calculations outlined in this chapter, but the earth pressure coefficients, particularly for the cell fill material, lie between the active and passive pressure conditions used for other retaining structures. Table 4-7 outlines several failure modes and specifics of the analysis methods for cofferdams. Details regarding the stability of sheet pile cofferdams, along with solutions to example problems, can be found in the USS Steel Sheet Piling Design Manual (USS 1984) and the Corps of Engineers' EM 1100-2-2503 (USACE 1989).

Table 4-7 details the following failure modes and design guidance:

SLIDING (base friction):
• Use F ≥ 1.25 for temporary structures; F ≥ 1.50 for permanent structures.
• F = (W'tanδ) / (PA + Pw), where W' = effective weight of backfill, Pw = net water pressure force, δ = interface friction angle along bottom (= 0.5 for smooth rock, = φ' for soil at base).

SLIDING (along weak seam):
• Location of failure plane must be assumed. Active and passive pressure calculated to top of weak seam. W' includes soil beneath sheet piles to top of weak seam.
• Use F ≥ 1.25 for temporary; F ≥ 1.50 for permanent.
• F = (W'tanφ' + c'B) / (PA + Pw), where φ' = effective stress friction angle of weak seam, c' = effective stress cohesion of weak seam.

OVERTURNING:
• Resultant force R must be located in the middle third of base. Calculate eccentricity and maintain |e| ≤ B/6.
• Note: This is not a realistic failure mode owing to the flexibility of the cofferdam structure; nonetheless, it is customary to still check overturning in cofferdam design.

ROTATION (Hansen method):
• Failure is assumed to occur on a logarithmic spiral surface. W' calculated by removing the area (A) below the failure surface. Critical surface found by trial and error or by locating using the point of application of W' and ΣP forces and the locus of poles. Use F ≥ 1.25 temporary, F ≥ 1.50 permanent.
• ΣP = PA + PP − PW and F = MB / Mω, where MB = moment about pole for W', Mω = moment about pole for ΣP.

DEEP SEATED SLIDING (Hansen method):
• Failure on a logarithmic spiral surface, may be inside or outside cofferdam. Interface friction angle (δ) between steel and soil used. Active and passive earth pressure forces assumed to act in reversed direction. Normally only horizontal component used. Critical surface found by trial and error. F ≥ 1.25 temporary, F ≥ 1.50 permanent.
• ΣP = PA + PP − PW and F = MB / Mω.

BEARING CAPACITY:
• Seepage into cofferdam can affect bearing capacity. Bearing capacity analysis performed in addition to rotational failure analysis. Use methods from Chapter 5. F ≥ 2.0 for sand (permanent and temporary); F ≥ 3.0 for clay (permanent and temporary).

SETTLEMENT:
• Settlement can increase tilt and overturning moment. Stress distribution varies horizontally and vertically. Estimate using elastic theory influence charts (DM7.1, Chapter 4). Consolidation settlement calculated per DM7.1 (Chapter 5).

INTERLOCK TENSION:
• Pressure caused by cell fill should not exceed allowable sheet pile interlock tension. Critical horizontal pressure assumed at H/4 above the point of fixity (alternatively, at top elevation of inboard berm). Use F = 2 to 4.
• For main cell: p = KA[γ'(H−H3) + γw(H−H3) + γ(H3−H4)] and tmax = p·R (where KA = 0.4, R = cell radius).
• For connections between main cell and connecting arcs: tmax = p·L·sec α.

VERTICAL SHEAR RESISTANCE (Terzaghi/pullout of outboard sheets):
• Outboard sheet piles can lift due to applied moment, causing loss of cell fill. Shear occurs between fill and sheet piles. F = resisting moment due to friction on outboard piling / overturning moment. Use F ≥ 1.5 for permanent structures.
• F = [W'tanδ(B/2 + e)] / [B(PA + PP)·H + PW·H].

HORIZONTAL SHEAR RESISTANCE (Cummings method):
• Tilting can cause excessive shear on a vertical plane through the centerline of cofferdam fill. Shear resistance of fill and frictional resistance of sheet pile interlocks must exceed applied shear stress. The earth pressure coefficient used is greater than active. Use F ≥ 1.5 for permanent structures.
• Total shear force Q = 3M / (2B), where M = net overturning moment.
key_points: Cofferdam geometries (circular, semicircular, cloverleaf) are converted to an equivalent parallel wall width B for hand calculations, where B gives the same sectional modulus as the actual cell.
Phreatic surface in cell fill is assumed at 1H:1V slope for free-draining coarse fill and 3H:1V for poorly-draining fine-grained fill; inboard water pressure stabilizing effects are often ignored.
Three main loading cases must be evaluated: Case I (max pool), Case II (initial filling), and Case III (drawdown conditions), each requiring assessment of up to 13 failure modes.
Earth pressure coefficients for cell fill lie between active and passive values; KA = 0.4 is used for interlock tension calculations.
Interlock tension: tmax = p·R for main cell; tmax = p·L·sec α for connections between main cell and connecting arcs.
Bearing capacity factors of safety: F ≥ 2.0 for sand, F ≥ 3.0 for clay; general F ≥ 1.25 (temporary) and F ≥ 1.50 (permanent) for sliding and rotation modes.
Horizontal shear force at centerline: Q = 3M / (2B), where M is the net overturning moment.
Numerical methods modeling soil-structure interaction are often used due to the complexity of cofferdam design; key references are USS 1984 and USACE EM 1110-2-2503 (1989).

equations.description: Factor of safety against sliding along base: F = W'tanδ / (PA + Pw), where W' = effective weight of backfill, Pw = net water pressure force, δ = interface friction angle along bottom.
Factor of safety against sliding along weak seam: F = (W'tanφ' + c'B) / (PA + Pw), where φ' and c' are effective strength parameters of the weak seam.
Eccentricity of resultant force: e = B/2 - x, where x is calculated from moment equilibrium of W', PA, and Pw about the base; must maintain |e| ≤ B/6.
Net lateral force for rotation analysis: ΣP = PA + PP − PW.
Factor of safety for rotation (Hansen method): F = MB / Mω, where MB = moment about pole for W', Mω = moment about pole for ΣP.
Maximum inboard sheeting pressure for interlock tension: p = KA[γ'(H−H3) + γw(H−H3) + γ(H3−H4)], using KA = 0.4.
Maximum interlock tension in main cell (lbs per linear inch): tmax = p · R, where R = cell radius.
Maximum interlock tension at connections between main cell and connecting arcs: tmax = p · L · sec α.
Factor of safety against pullout of outboard sheets (vertical shear, Terzaghi method): F = [W'tanδ(B/2 + e)] / [B(PA + PP)H + PWH].
Total shear force on vertical plane through centerline (Cummings method): Q = 3M / (2B), where M = net overturning moment.

sections.title: Cofferdam Retardation of Corrosion
sections.summary: Addresses corrosion protection requirements for cofferdams used as permanent structures, particularly in brackish or seawater environments. Identifies the critical corrosion zone from the top of the splash zone to just below mean low water level, and specifies mitigation measures including protective coatings, corrosion-resistant steel, and cathodic protection.
sections.body: When cofferdams are used as permanent structures, particularly in brackish water or seawater, severe corrosion occurs from top of the splash zone to a point just below mean low water level. Use protective coatings, corrosion resistant steel, and/or cathodic protection in these areas.
key_points: Severe corrosion zone spans from the top of the splash zone to just below mean low water level in brackish or seawater environments.
Applicable when cofferdams serve as permanent structures rather than temporary construction aids.
Mitigation options include protective coatings, corrosion-resistant steel, and/or cathodic protection.
All three protective measures may be used in combination depending on severity of exposure.
sections.applicability: Applies when cofferdams are used as permanent structures in brackish water or seawater environments subject to corrosion.

sections.title: Problem Soils and Retaining Walls
sections.summary: References Chapter 1 for a broad summary of problem soil conditions affecting foundation and earth structure design, and directs the reader to Table 4-8, which summarizes key design considerations for retaining walls in problem soil conditions. Serves as a cross-reference hub for applying problem-soil guidance specifically to retaining wall design.
sections.body: Chapter 1 provides a summary of many types of problem soil conditions that can affect the design of foundations and earth structures. Table 4-8 summarizes important conditions for the design of retaining walls in problem soils.
key_points: Chapter 1 is the primary reference for identifying and characterizing problem soil conditions relevant to foundations and earth structures.
Table 4-8 consolidates critical problem-soil design considerations specifically for retaining walls.
Engineers should consult both Chapter 1 and Table 4-8 together when designing retaining walls on or in problem soils.
Problem soils can significantly influence retaining wall design approach, materials, and performance requirements.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing retaining walls in or on problem soil conditions as identified in Chapter 1 of UFC 3-220-20.

sections.title: NOTATION
sections.summary: Comprehensive notation table for Chapter 4 (Retaining Structures) of UFC 3-220-20, defining all variables used throughout the chapter. Covers earth pressure coefficients (KA, KP, K0, KAE), resultant forces (PA, PP, PAE, PH, PT), seismic and hydrodynamic pressure terms, compaction pressures, geometric and strength parameters, and Greek-letter symbols for angles, unit weights, stresses, and flexibility.
sections.body:

σʹz — Effective vertical stress
θ — Angle of the wall face on the retained side
key_points: Defines all variables used in Chapter 4, covering earth pressure coefficients (KA, KP, K0, KAE), safety factors (FOT, FSL), and resultant force symbols (PA, PP, PAE, PH, PT, Pv).

Seismic terms include KAE (seismic active earth pressure coefficient), PAE (seismic active earth pressure force), kh (horizontal ground acceleration), kv (vertical ground acceleration), and ∆PAE (seismic-induced increase in active pressure).
Water and hydrodynamic pressure symbols: pw (hydrodynamic), Pw, PwA, PwP, u, and U are distinguished to allow precise accounting of water forces on each side of a wall.
The symbol q is used for three distinct compaction pressure sources (vibratory plate tamper, rammer plate, roller) as well as uniform surcharge — context determines which definition applies.
Seepage effects are captured by ∆PA and ∆PP (changes in active and passive resultant forces due to seepage) and pore pressure coefficient ru.

Greek symbols cover interface friction (δ), backfill slope (β), wall face angle (θ), Coulomb failure plane angles (αA, αP), unit weights (γ, γb, γeq, γsat), stress components (σʹh, σʹz, σʹHθ), and flexibility number (ρ).
Strength parameters include cʹ, φ, φʹ, φʹallow, su, and su,F, supporting both total-stress and effective-stress analysis approaches used throughout the chapter.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever interpreting or working with any equation, figure, or table in Chapter 4 of UFC 3-220-20 that uses the defined variable symbols.

sections.summary: Curated reference list for Chapter 4 topics including anchored bulkheads, apparent earth pressures, ground anchors, soil nail walls, mechanically stabilized earth walls, and cofferdams. key_points: USS (1984) Steel Sheet Piling Design Manual is the primary reference for anchored bulkhead design.
FHWA GEC No. 4 (FHWA-IF-99-015, 1999) covers apparent earth pressures, ground anchors, and soil nail walls.
FHWA-NHI-10-024/025 (2009) provides design and construction guidance for mechanically stabilized earth walls and reinforced soil slopes in two volumes.
USACE EM 1110-2-2503 (1989) is the key reference for cofferdam and sheet pile cellular structure design.
Also lists symbol definitions for θP (obtuse angle between critical Coulomb failure plane and vertical) and ψ (horizontal acceleration angle for seismic loading).
